answer.event: While Rav Hamnuna studied before Ulla, Ulla praised him but lamented that he came from Harpanya, a town of flawed lineage.
answer.turn: Rav Hamnuna was ashamed; Ulla asked where he paid his poll tax and learned it was Pum Nahara.
answer.outcome: Ulla declared that he was therefore from Pum Nahara, clearing his lineage.
answer.summary: Rav Hamnuna was studying before Ulla, who exclaimed what a great man he was, if only he were not from Harpanya, a town known for flawed lineage. Rav Hamnuna was embarrassed. Ulla asked him where he paid his poll tax, and he answered Pum Nahara. Ulla concluded that he was then really from Pum Nahara, and his lineage was sound.

answer.event: A case about an alleyway closed by the sea on one side and a garbage dump on the other came before Rabbi.
answer.turn: Rabbi declined to rule either way.
answer.outcome: He said neither prohibition nor permission.
answer.summary: There was an alleyway with the sea at one end and a garbage dump at the other, and the question of whether one could carry in it came before Rabbi. He gave no ruling at all, neither forbidding nor permitting it.
answer.missing: Any reaction or consequence of the non-ruling; the reasoning given afterward is commentary, not narrative.

answer.actor: A man in Mata Mehasya and his brother
answer.event: A man's brother tried to disqualify the man's yevama by giving her a bill of divorce, fearing being cheated over the dead brother's property.
answer.turn: The man offered to divide the property, and when the brother feared a swindle like the one in Pumbedita, offered to let him take his share immediately.
answer.summary: A man in Mata Mehasya was due to marry his late brother's widow, but another brother wanted to disqualify her with a bill of divorce. The man asked why, offering to share the estate. The brother said he feared being cheated as the Pumbedita swindler had cheated his brother, so the man offered to let him take his share right away.
answer.missing: How the dispute ended; the passage moves into legal discussion of the offer.

answer.event: Walking on the road with a woman ahead of them, Rav urged Rav Yehuda to hurry away from her.
answer.turn: Rav Yehuda cited Rav's own ruling that men of good morals may be together with a woman; Rav said that did not mean the two of them.
answer.outcome: Rav explained it applied only to people like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues.
answer.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were walking along a road with a woman ahead of them. Rav told Rav Yehuda to quicken his steps away from Gehenna. Rav Yehuda objected that Rav himself had permitted this for men of good character, but Rav replied that he had not meant men like them, only men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues.

answer.actor: Rabba bar Avuh and Rav Nahman
answer.event: Rabba bar Avuh told the Sages to examine Rav Nahman in the bath, and if his flesh gave off steam he would give him his daughter.
answer.summary: Rabba bar Avuh instructed the Sages to watch Rav Nahman while he bathed, promising that if his body gave off steam (showing he was not impotent) he would give him his daughter in marriage.
answer.missing: Whether the examination happened and what came of it; the passage cites the instruction only for a legal point.

answer.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with beer sediment belonging to his employer.
answer.turn: The owner found him and asked why he had not used the better sediment, and the brewer asked Rava whether this meant consent.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled that such a remark counts as consent only for teruma, so the brewer had no right to the sediment.
answer.summary: A brewer making beer for someone betrothed a woman with some of the beer's sediment. The owner found him and asked why he had not used the better, sharper sediment instead. The brewer asked Rava whether this showed the owner's consent, making the betrothal valid. Rava said that remark signals consent only in matters of teruma, not here.

answer.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged in the street by a pig.
answer.turn: He exclaimed that a mouth that produced pearls should not lick dust.
answer.outcome: He went out and sinned.
answer.summary: According to one account, Elisha ben Avuya, known as Aher, saw the tongue of the executed scholar Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged along by a pig. Appalled, he cried out that a mouth which had produced pearls should not lick the dust. Because of this he went out and abandoned the path, sinning.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin (or Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Zevida), and Ameimar
answer.event: A visiting sage ruled on the offspring of a slave and a Jewish woman in Rav Gazza's town.
answer.turn: Reports conflict over who the sage was and whether he declared the offspring of a married woman unfit.
answer.outcome: Another report says Ameimar visited and declared the offspring fit in both cases.
answer.summary: Rav Gazza reported that a visiting sage came to his town and ruled on two cases of children born to Jewish women from slaves: fit if the mother was unmarried, unfit if married. Another version says the sage was a different Rabbi Yosei who declared both fit. Separately, Ameimar visited another town and also declared the offspring fit in both cases.
answer.missing: Any turn beyond the rulings themselves; these are reports of decisions rather than a developed narrative.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Elazar and Reish Lakish
answer.event: Rabbi Yohanan taught a ruling about burning notar and Rabbi Elazar refuted him from a baraita.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan, silenced, praised Rabbi Elazar as expounding like Moses, but Reish Lakish revealed it was a baraita from Torat Kohanim.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan went and learned Torat Kohanim in three days and mastered it in three months.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yohanan was teaching that leftover sacrificial meat burned after its time may be burned at night. Rabbi Elazar challenged him with a teaching that the verse extends the daytime requirement, and Rabbi Yohanan fell silent. Afterward he told Reish Lakish he had seen ben Pedat expound like Moses from God's mouth, but Reish Lakish said it was not original, it was a baraita from Torat Kohanim. Rabbi Yohanan then learned that whole work in three days and understood it in three months.

answer.event: While Rabbi Yehuda and others sat before Rabbi Tarfon, a yevama came to perform halitza.
answer.turn: Rabbi Tarfon instructed all present to respond 'He who had his shoe removed.'
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled sitting with others before Rabbi Tarfon when a widow came to perform the halitza ceremony. Rabbi Tarfon told everyone present to call out together, 'He who had his shoe removed.'
answer.missing: Whether they did so or anything that followed; the incident is cited as a source for a practice.

answer.event: Rabba bar Hiyya conducted a halitza with a non-leather slipper, alone, and at night.
answer.turn: Shmuel criticized him for relying on individual minority opinions.
answer.outcome: The act stood under Shmuel's sarcastic rebuke.
answer.summary: Rabba bar Hiyya from Ctesiphon performed a halitza ceremony using a slipper, as the sole judge, and at night. Shmuel remarked sarcastically on how bold this master was to follow lone opinions in his practice.

answer.actor: Mar Yehuda and Rav Huna bar Yehuda
answer.event: Visiting Rav Huna bar Yehuda's house, Mar Yehuda saw people carrying among trees not planted in rows.
answer.turn: He challenged Rav Huna for not following Avimi's view.
answer.outcome: Rav Huna answered that he followed Rav Nahman, who permits it.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda visited the home of Rav Huna bar Yehuda and saw people carrying on Shabbat in an enclosure whose trees were not planted in rows. He asked whether Rav Huna did not accept Avimi's ruling forbidding this. Rav Huna replied that he followed Rav Nahman, who permitted it.

answer.event: In Rabbi Pedat's house a beam so heavy it took ten people to lift was placed against the door to secure it.
answer.turn: Rabbi Pedat said nothing against it.
answer.outcome: He explained that it had the status of a utensil.
answer.summary: In Rabbi Pedat's house there was a huge beam that took ten people to lift, and they would set it against the door to secure it. Rabbi Pedat never objected, explaining that the beam counted as a utensil and could be used this way on Shabbat.
answer.missing: It describes a recurring practice rather than a single event with a turn.

answer.actor: Rav Mordekhai (reporting) and a divorced woman
answer.event: A bill of divorce lay closer to the woman than the husband and was lost.
answer.outcome: They required her to undergo halitza.
answer.summary: Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi of a case where a bill of divorce landed closer to a woman than to her husband but never reached her hand. When the husband died, the rabbis required her to undergo halitza because her divorce was in doubt.
answer.missing: Names, circumstances and the course of the case; it is a bare report of a ruling.

answer.event: A man walked past the door of his father-in-law's house.
answer.turn: He was suspected of an affair with his mother-in-law.
answer.outcome: Rav Sheshet had him flogged.
answer.summary: A certain man passed by the entrance of his father-in-law's house and Rav Sheshet had him lashed. The reason was that he was suspected of a relationship with his mother-in-law.
answer.missing: Only a bare report of the incident, cited to resolve a legal question.

answer.event: Rav Kahana, a priest, took a cloth as payment for a firstborn's redemption.
answer.turn: He declared that to him the cloth was worth five sela.
answer.outcome: The redemption was accepted with the cloth.
answer.summary: Rav Kahana, a priest, accepted a cloth at a firstborn son's redemption ceremony, telling the father that to him the cloth was worth the required five sela. A related report tells that Mar bar Rav Ashi paid thirteen dinars for a cloth worth ten.
answer.missing: Little beyond the act and statement; both incidents are cited as legal precedents.

answer.actor: A yavam and yevama; Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: A couple performed halitza privately in a prison and the case came before Rabbi Akiva, who validated it.
answer.turn: The Gemara explains it was valid because witnesses saw it from outside, and that both the act and the ruling took place in prison.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Akiva validated the halitza.
answer.summary: A man and his brother's widow performed halitza between themselves while in prison, and the case was brought to Rabbi Akiva, himself imprisoned, who ruled it valid. The Gemara adds that witnesses watched from outside, and that both the ceremony and the ruling happened in the prison.
answer.missing: The incident itself is told in the mishna, which is only cited here; the passage is discussion of its details.

answer.actor: Rav Malkiyyu and a deaf-mute neighbor
answer.event: Rav Malkiyyu married his deaf-mute neighbor to a woman and wrote her a 400-dinar marriage contract from the deaf-mute's property.
answer.turn: Although a deaf-mute is not obligated to give a marriage contract, Rav Malkiyyu reasoned that a wife serves him even better than a maidservant they would buy him.
answer.outcome: Rava praised Rav Malkiyyu as a great and wise man.
answer.summary: A deaf-mute lived near Rav Malkiyyu, who arranged a marriage for him and wrote the wife a 400-dinar marriage contract out of the deaf-mute's property. Rav Malkiyyu reasoned that if the man needed a maidservant they would buy him one, so all the more a wife. Rava praised him as a wise and great man.

answer.event: An uncircumcised priest sprinkled the purification waters.
answer.outcome: The Sages validated his sprinkling.
answer.summary: A baraita reports that an uncircumcised priest once sprinkled the purification waters, and the Sages ruled his sprinkling valid.
answer.missing: Any detail of the incident: who, where, or how it came before the Sages; it is only a bare report attached to a rule.

answer.event: Ravnai came to sell sesame and reported Shmuel's ruling that a witness and judge combine.
answer.turn: Ameimar praised the ruling, and Rav Ashi retorted that he praised it only because his grandfather did, and that Rava had refuted it.
answer.outcome: The ruling is declared already refuted.
answer.summary: Ravnai, brother of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, came to sell sesame and passed on Shmuel's ruling that a witness and a judge may join together. Ameimar praised the ruling, but Rav Ashi teased him that he only praised it because his maternal grandfather had, and noted that Rava had already refuted it.
answer.missing: Mostly a chain of reported sayings; the only event is Ravnai's arrival.

answer.actor: A man who deposited a silver goblet; Hasa; Rav Nahman
answer.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without saying anything about it.
answer.turn: The depositor claimed it before Rav Nahman, who knew Hasa was not wealthy and noted the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the claimant, provided he was not a regular visitor to the house.
answer.summary: A man left a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without leaving instructions about it. The parties came to Rav Nahman, who reasoned that Hasa was not rich enough to own such a goblet and that the claimant could describe its marks, so it was his. He added that this holds only if the claimant was not a frequent visitor who might have just seen it there.

answer.event: Bonyos sent Rabbi a se'a measure from Na'usa.
answer.turn: Rabbi measured it.
answer.outcome: It held 217 eggs.
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported that a man named Bonyos sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a se'a measuring vessel from Na'usa. Rabbi measured its volume and found it held 217 eggs.

answer.event: The Sages urged Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to marry and have children.
answer.turn: He refused, saying he would have had children from his first wife had he merited; the real reason was that he had become impotent from Rav Huna's long discourses.
answer.outcome: He did not remarry.
answer.summary: The Sages told Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to marry again and have children. He brushed them off, saying that if he were worthy he would already have had children with his first wife. The Gemara reveals the real reason: he had become impotent from holding himself in during Rav Huna's lengthy lectures.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
answer.event: Rabbi Yehoshua went to study with Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri and found him sitting among trees.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua stretched a vine between two trees and asked whether one could sow diverse kinds on the other side.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri answered: permitted if ten cubits apart, prohibited if more.
answer.summary: Though already expert in the laws of diverse kinds, Rabbi Yehoshua went to learn Torah from Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri and found him sitting among trees. Rabbi Yehoshua stretched a vine from tree to tree and asked whether seeds could be sown beyond it if grapevines grew inside. Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri ruled it permitted if the trees were ten cubits apart and forbidden if farther.

answer.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava; Rav Nehemya
answer.event: The widow came before Rav Nehemya asking him to allot her sustenance.
answer.turn: She then asked for wine as well.
answer.outcome: He granted it, since the people of Mehoza drink wine.
answer.summary: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava came to Rav Nehemya son of Rav Yosef and asked him to set her sustenance, which he did. She then asked for a wine allowance too, and he granted it, explaining that Mehoza residents customarily drink wine.

answer.actor: A man who deposited sesame and the bailee
answer.event: A man deposited sesame with a friend and later asked for it back.
answer.turn: The friend claimed he had already returned it; the owner pointed to sesame of the stated amount in a barrel, and the friend said that was different sesame.
answer.summary: A man left sesame with a friend and later asked for it. The friend said he had already taken it back. The owner said it was a specific amount stored in a barrel, but the friend insisted the sesame in the barrel was someone else's.
answer.missing: The ruling: the context only says Rav Hisda thought to rule a certain way, without the final decision.

answer.event: The court of priests set a 100-dinar marriage contract for priestly widows, then raised it to 200 when the widows were treated with disrespect.
answer.turn: Men then stopped marrying priestly widows, preferring Israelite virgins for the same price.
answer.outcome: The court restored the original amount.
answer.summary: The priestly court first fixed a marriage contract of 100 dinars for a priest's widowed daughter. Seeing such widows treated with contempt, they raised it to 200. But men then avoided them, preferring to marry an Israelite virgin for the same sum, so the court went back to the original amount.

answer.actor: A superintendent; his neighbors; Rav Yehuda
answer.event: The neighbors asked a superintendent to rent them his domain for an eiruv, and he refused.
answer.turn: They asked whether they could rent from his wife; Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya and Rav Mattana had no answer.
answer.outcome: Rav Yehuda cited Shmuel that a man's wife may make an eiruv without his knowledge.
answer.summary: A superintendent living near Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya refused to rent his domain to his neighbors so they could carry on Shabbat. They asked whether they could rent it from his wife instead; neither Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya nor Rav Mattana knew. Finally Rav Yehuda told them, in Shmuel's name, that a wife may join an eiruv without her husband's knowledge.

answer.event: Rav Yosef, having forgotten his learning, said he had never heard a teaching of Shmuel about roofs.
answer.turn: Abaye reminded him he had taught it to them, quoting it; Rav Yosef then recalled it differently.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef restated the teaching in his own corrected version, reconciling Abaye's mention of residents.
answer.summary: After an illness made him forget, Rav Yosef said he had never heard Shmuel's ruling about adjacent roofs. His student Abaye told him he had taught it to them himself and recited the version he remembered. Rav Yosef then remembered and said he had taught it differently, and when Abaye pressed him on the word 'residents', he explained what he had meant.

answer.event: A large unenclosed yard in Pum Nahara opened to the town and to a vineyard path leading to a river.
answer.turn: Abaye rejected two solutions and proposed a side post at the vineyard path; Rava objected that people would draw a wrong conclusion.
answer.outcome: Rava proposed placing the side post at the opening to the town.
answer.summary: A yard in Pum Nahara could not be carried in on Shabbat. Abaye weighed a partition on the river bank and a doorframe at the path, rejecting both, and suggested a side post at the vineyard path. Rava objected that people would wrongly think a side post works for any vineyard path, and proposed instead a side post at the yard's opening to the town.
answer.missing: Little happens beyond the sages' deliberation; whether the solution was carried out is not stated.

answer.actor: A millstone owner and the renter
answer.event: A man rented his millstone to another in exchange for grinding services.
answer.turn: The owner grew rich, bought his own millstone and donkey, and demanded money instead; the renter insisted he would only grind.
answer.summary: A man rented out his millstone, to be paid by the renter grinding his grain. Later the owner became rich, bought another millstone and a donkey, and asked for cash rent. The renter refused, saying he had agreed to grind, not to pay money.
answer.missing: The resolution; the following context only gives Ravina's initial legal comparison.

answer.actor: A man who deposited silk; Rav Dimi; Rabbi Abba
answer.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without leaving instructions.
answer.turn: The claimant came before Rabbi Abba, who knew Rav Dimi was not wealthy and noted the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Abba ruled the silk belonged to the claimant, unless he was a regular visitor.
answer.summary: A man left silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who then died without saying anything about it. Rabbi Abba ruled the silk belonged to the claimant, since Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant could identify it. He added that this holds only if the claimant did not frequent the house.

answer.actor: Shmuel and a man with a case
answer.event: While Shmuel was getting off a ferry, a man gave him a hand.
answer.turn: Shmuel asked what he was doing there and learned the man had a case to bring before him.
answer.outcome: Shmuel declared himself disqualified from judging the case.
answer.summary: Shmuel was crossing a river on a ferry when a man helped him out by the hand. Shmuel asked why he was there, and the man said he had a lawsuit for Shmuel to judge. Shmuel told him that the small favor now disqualified him from hearing the case.

answer.event: Rav Safra challenged Rava on why Akistefon and Ardeshir are treated as one city despite the Tigris separating them.
answer.turn: Rava went out and showed him submerged wall foundations in the river.
answer.outcome: The foundations linked the cities within seventy-odd cubits, answering the challenge.
answer.summary: Rav Safra asked Rava how the Shabbat limits of Akistefon and Ardeshir could be measured as if they were one city, when the Tigris separated them by more than the allowed distance. Rava took him out and showed him the remains of a city wall submerged in the river, reaching to within about seventy cubits of the other city.

answer.event: A woman who had seized a silver cup toward her marriage contract also demanded sustenance from the orphans.
answer.turn: She came before Rava for judgment.
answer.outcome: Rava ordered the orphans to give her sustenance.
answer.summary: A widow took a silver cup as partial payment of her marriage contract and also demanded continued support. She brought the case to Rava, who told the orphans to pay her sustenance, since no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view that partial payment counts as full payment.

answer.event: When Rav Nahman came to Neharde'a, he ordered the earth blocking the alleyway doors cleared away.
answer.summary: Some alleyway doors in Neharde'a were partly blocked with earth. When Rav Nahman arrived, he ordered the earth cleared so the doors could be shut.
answer.missing: Whether the order was carried out or what followed; the rest is legal analysis of his instruction.

answer.event: Rabbi Elazar missed the study hall one day and asked Rabbi Asi what had been said there.
answer.turn: Rabbi Asi reported Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Elazar learned the ruling and drew an inference from it.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar did not attend the study hall one day. Meeting Rabbi Asi, he asked what the Sages had said, and Rabbi Asi told him Rabbi Yochanan ruled like Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Elazar inferred from this that some individual must disagree, and Rabbi Asi confirmed it.
answer.missing: The exchange is mostly a vehicle for transmitting a ruling; little happens beyond the question and answer.

answer.actor: Rabbi Zeira's neighbors and a gentile superintendent
answer.event: A gentile superintendent refused to rent his domain to his Jewish neighbors for an eiruv, so they asked Rabbi Zeira whether they could rent it from his wife.
answer.turn: Rabbi Zeira cited Rabbi Hanina's ruling that a man's wife may make an eiruv without his knowledge.
answer.outcome: The neighbors were permitted to rent the domain from the wife.
answer.summary: A gentile official living near Rabbi Zeira refused to rent his property to the neighbors so they could carry on Shabbat. They asked Rabbi Zeira whether they could rent it from his wife instead. He answered, citing Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Hanina, that a wife may establish an eiruv without her husband's knowledge, so they could.

answer.actor: A man whose betrothed died; Rav Nahman's circle; Rav Hiyya bar Ami
answer.event: A man whose betrothed had died came before the sages, who told him to bury her or pay her marriage contract.
answer.turn: Rav Hiyya bar Ami objected, citing a teaching that a man has no mourning or inheritance obligations for a betrothed wife.
answer.summary: Several sages were sitting together when a man came whose betrothed wife had died. They told him to bury her or pay her marriage contract. Rav Hiyya bar Ami challenged them with a mishna stating that a betrothed husband neither mourns nor inherits from her. The text does not say what the man finally did.
answer.missing: How the case was resolved for the man; the passage turns into legal analysis.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok and his family, descendants of Sena'av ben Binyamin
answer.event: When the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat, the family postponed the fast to Sunday.
answer.turn: Sunday was their family festival day.
answer.outcome: They fasted but did not complete the fast because of their festival.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok recalled that his family, descendants of Sena'av ben Binyamin, kept a family festival. Once the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat and the fast was pushed to Sunday, which was their festival. They fasted that day but broke off before evening because it was their holiday.

answer.event: Rav came to Damharya and issued a practical ruling about a breach in an alleyway.
answer.turn: Rav Hanan bar Rava argued the ruling was a special stringency because Rav found an unguarded valley.
answer.summary: Rav Huna claimed that Rav, visiting Damharya, had ruled according to Rav Huna's view. Rav Hanan bar Rava replied that Rav had found the place lax and added a safeguard there. The incident is only cited as evidence in a legal dispute.
answer.missing: The details of the Damharya incident itself; it is only alluded to.

answer.actor: A man who fell into the Great Cistern
answer.event: A man fell into the Great Cistern and emerged after three days.
answer.outcome: He survived, which the Sages called a miracle not to be used for halakha.
answer.summary: Rabbi Meir cited the case of a man who fell into a great cistern and came out alive three days later. The Sages replied that one does not cite miracles as legal precedent. The incident itself is only referenced, not told.
answer.missing: The narrative of the fall and rescue is only mentioned by reference to the mishna.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman in the marketplace with a myrtle branch, and Rav Aha bar Huna sent the case to Rav Yosef.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef ruled the man should be flogged and the woman should need a divorce.
answer.outcome: The man was to be flogged per Rav, and a bill of divorce required per Shmuel.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman in the marketplace using a myrtle branch. Rav Aha bar Huna sent the question to Rav Yosef. Rav Yosef replied that the man should be flogged for his crude conduct, and that the woman needed a bill of divorce in case the branch had some value.

answer.event: People came before Rabbi Ami with a bill of divorce lacking witnesses.
answer.outcome: He told them to complete it even with a slave from the market.
answer.summary: People brought Rabbi Ami a case of a bill of divorce that needed more witnesses. He told them to go and complete it even with a slave from the public. It is a bare report of a ruling.
answer.missing: Who came and what the case was is only implied.

answer.event: The Rabbis urged Rav Sheshet to marry and have sons.
answer.turn: He replied that his daughter's sons were his sons, but in truth he had become impotent from Rav Huna's long discourses.
answer.outcome: He put them off and did not remarry.
answer.summary: The Rabbis told Rav Sheshet he should marry and father sons. He answered that his grandsons through his daughter counted as his sons. The Gemara explains he was only deflecting them: he had become impotent from waiting through Rav Huna's very long lectures.

answer.actor: A depositor and the family of Rabbi Meyasha
answer.event: A man deposited seven pearls wrapped in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without telling his household whose they were.
answer.turn: Rabbi Ami knew Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy, and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the claimant.
answer.summary: A man left seven pearls tied in a sheet at the home of Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Rabbi Meyasha died without saying whose they were, and the dispute came to Rabbi Ami. He ruled for the claimant, since he knew Rabbi Meyasha could not have afforded such gems and the claimant could describe them.

answer.event: Shimon ben Azzai found a genealogy scroll in Jerusalem.
answer.turn: It recorded a mamzer, praise of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teachings, and that Manasseh killed Isaiah.
answer.summary: Shimon ben Azzai reported finding a scroll of lineages in Jerusalem. Among its entries were that a certain man was a mamzer, that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teachings were few but reliable, and that King Manasseh killed the prophet Isaiah. Beyond the finding, the passage is a list of contents.
answer.missing: The Manasseh-Isaiah story is only stated as a fact here; its telling begins in the following segment.

answer.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
answer.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land, and Rav bought it for himself.
answer.turn: The land lay among violent people who respected Rav but not Rabba bar bar Hana, and Rav feared someone else would buy it meanwhile.
answer.outcome: Rav kept the land without first informing Rabba bar bar Hana.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a field for him, but Rav bought it for himself. The Gemara explains that the field was in a valley of violent men who would sell to Rav but not to Rabba bar bar Hana. Rav did not stop to tell him first, fearing that another buyer would get it in the meantime.

answer.event: In a good mood, Abaye boasted that he was like ben Azzai, ready for any question.
answer.turn: A Sage challenged him on why the redemption verses are read leniently.
answer.outcome: Abaye answered from the Torah's leniency toward a Hebrew slave; the debate continues.
answer.summary: Abaye once declared himself as sharp as ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias. A scholar immediately tested him: why read the verses about redeeming a Hebrew slave leniently rather than stringently? Abaye answered that the Torah is consistently lenient toward such a slave. The rest is legal argument.
answer.missing: The exchange has no narrative ending; it continues as legal debate.

answer.event: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer and then Rabbi Yehoshua whom to serve first if both parents ask for water.
answer.turn: When he asked about a divorced mother, Rabbi Yehoshua saw from his tearful eyes that he was a widow's son.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua answered him sarcastically to pour water in a basin and call them like chickens.
answer.summary: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer whether father or mother comes first if both ask for water, and was told the father. He asked Rabbi Yehoshua and got the same answer, then asked what if the mother were divorced. Rabbi Yehoshua noticed his tear-filled eyes, realized he had no living father, and mocked the pointless question: pour water in a bowl and cluck for them like chickens.

answer.event: Rabbi Shabbtai's widowed daughter-in-law seized a saddlebag full of coins for her sustenance.
answer.outcome: The Sages had no power to take it from her.
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law grabbed a saddlebag full of coins to support herself. The Sages found they had no legal authority to take it back from her.

answer.actor: Two claimants to a field and Rav Yosef
answer.event: Two deeds of sale for the same property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one just 'Nisan'.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef awarded the field to the dated deed, and the loser asked for an authorization to repossess from Iyyar on.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef refused, since buyers could claim his deed was from the first of Nisan.
answer.summary: Two men brought Rav Yosef deeds to the same field, one dated the fifth of Nisan, the other only 'Nisan'. Rav Yosef gave it to the man with the exact date. The loser protested and asked for a writ letting him seize property sold from Iyyar on, but Rav Yosef answered that buyers could say his deed was from the first of Nisan and so the field was his to chase.

answer.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
answer.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to test whether he would become angry.
answer.summary: Rav Huna deliberately tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether the son would lose his temper. The Gemara discusses whether this was permitted, noting he had waived his honor. The text does not say how the son reacted.
answer.missing: The son's reaction and how the test ended.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
answer.event: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua conducted a halitza before five judges.
answer.outcome: They did so to publicize the matter.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua performed a halitza ceremony with five judges rather than three. The Gemara explains they did this only to make the event publicly known. It is a bare report of a practice.

answer.event: Rav Yehuda ruled in a case about a bundle of branches.
answer.outcome: He treated it as consumption of the wife's property.
answer.summary: The judges of Pumbedita reported that Rav Yehuda once decided a case involving bundles of vine branches. The ruling is cited only to show his consistent legal view.
answer.missing: The facts of the case are supplied by the translation, not the text.

answer.actor: A man who sold land to Rav Pappa
answer.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed money to buy oxen.
answer.turn: In the end he did not need the money.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land to him, beyond the letter of the law.
answer.summary: A man sold a field to Rav Pappa to raise money for oxen. In the end he did not need the money, and Rav Pappa gave him back his land. The Gemara notes Rav Pappa did this beyond what the law required.

answer.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
answer.event: While the sages were reclining in the upper room of the house of Nit'za in Lod, they were asked whether study or action is greater.
answer.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action is greater, but Rabbi Akiva said study is greater.
answer.outcome: All of them agreed that study is greater, because study leads to action.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were gathered in an upper room in Lod when someone asked them whether study or action is greater. Rabbi Tarfon answered that action is greater; Rabbi Akiva answered that study is greater. In the end everyone agreed with Akiva, on the grounds that study leads to action.

answer.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, burdened with their father's widow's daily medical costs, asked him for advice, and he told them to fix a lump sum with the doctor.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan came to regret the advice, feeling he had acted like a legal advocate for his own family.
answer.outcome: He concluded that a man of stature is different and should not help relatives in a way that harms another.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had to pay for their father's widow, who needed treatment every day. They came to him for advice, and he told them to set a fixed fee with the doctor, which would shift the cost onto her marriage settlement. Afterward he regretted it, saying he had made himself like a lawyer, since an important person should not appear to favor his relatives.

answer.actor: Ravina and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
answer.event: Ravina found Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on a door bar, puzzling over a legal question.
answer.outcome: The question was left unresolved.
answer.summary: Ravina came upon Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on the bar of a door, deep in thought over whether a husband who simply says a divorce document is 'void' cancels it. No answer is recorded, and the question stands.
answer.missing: Any interaction or development beyond the scene of the sage pondering.

answer.event: Ben Nappaha owned houses in five courtyards in Usha, and his case came before the Sages.
answer.outcome: The Sages ruled that only his place of residence restricts carrying.
answer.summary: Ben Nappaha had houses in five courtyards in Usha, only one of which he lived in. The question of whether he restricted carrying in all of them came before the Sages, who ruled that only the place where he actually lived counted.
answer.missing: Anything beyond a bare case and its ruling.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Yohanan, Rav Shemen bar Abba
answer.event: Similar cases about a deserted wife's sustenance came before Rabbi in Beit She'arim and Rabbi Yishmael in Tzippori, who ruled differently.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan wondered at the ruling that denied her sustenance, and Rav Shemen bar Abba told him Shmuel had already explained it as a case where the husband was reported dead.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan expressed astonishment at how far they had analyzed it.
answer.summary: Two similar cases of a woman whose husband had gone abroad came before Rabbi and before Rabbi Yishmael, and one granted her sustenance while the other did not. Rabbi Yohanan was puzzled by the refusal. Rav Shemen bar Abba told him that Shmuel in Babylonia had explained it as a case where the husband was reported dead, and Rabbi Yohanan was amazed. A second version swaps which judge ruled which way.
answer.missing: The facts of the cases themselves are only alluded to; the exchange is mostly legal interpretation.

answer.actor: A man captured with his mother; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: A man casually remarked that he and his mother had been taken captive and that he had never stopped watching over her.
answer.turn: Though a son cannot normally testify for his mother, his remark was unconsidered and incidental.
answer.outcome: Rabbi permitted his mother to marry a priest on the basis of his words.
answer.summary: A man chatting offhandedly said that he and his mother had been held captive among gentiles, and that whether drawing water or gathering wood his mind was always on his mother. Because he said it in passing rather than as testimony, Rabbi accepted it and allowed his mother to marry into the priesthood.

answer.event: A man prepared a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after the woman's husband died.
answer.turn: Rava prohibited it.
answer.outcome: The man lost his feast.
answer.summary: A man arranged a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after his bride's first husband had died, and Rava stopped it, so the feast went to waste. The Gemara then explains it was really a wedding feast, not a betrothal.
answer.missing: Any detail beyond a one-line report used as a legal proof.

answer.event: A man told Rabbi Ami that someone had a presumption of priesthood because he read first in the synagogue.
answer.turn: Rabbi Ami questioned whether he read first as a priest or as a great man, and the witness showed a Levite read after him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami confirmed the man as a priest on his word.
answer.summary: A man came to Rabbi Ami claiming that another was known to be a priest because he was called first to the Torah. Rabbi Ami pressed him: perhaps he was honored as a scholar, not as a priest. The witness answered that a Levite was called right after him, and Rabbi Ami accepted the man as a priest.

answer.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain teaching.
answer.turn: His student Abaye reminded him that Rav Yosef himself had taught it to them, and in what context.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain ruling. Abaye told him that he had in fact taught it to them himself, reconstructing the discussion in which he had cited it. The passage does not say how Rav Yosef responded.
answer.missing: Rav Yosef's reaction; the cause of his forgetting is given only in the translator's gloss.

answer.actor: Rav Avya and his wife, sister of Rami bar Hama
answer.event: The sister of Rami bar Hama was married to Rav Avya, and her marriage contract was lost.
answer.turn: They came before Rav Yosef, who cited a ruling that it is Rabbi Meir's view that living without a full marriage contract is forbidden.
answer.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya, and her marriage contract was lost. The couple went to Rav Yosef, who told them that the view that such a marriage is improper belongs to Rabbi Meir. The resolution is not shown.
answer.missing: The passage itself is only the opening line; the rest of the story and its ending lie beyond the text shown.

answer.event: Rav Kahana held beer belonging to the orphan Rav Mesharshiyya bar Hilkai and delayed selling it until the Festival.
answer.outcome: He explained that even if it soured somewhat, it would fetch ready cash at the Festival.
answer.summary: Rav Kahana was holding beer that belonged to an orphan and waited until the Festival to sell it. He explained that even if it went a little sour, it would sell for good cash then.
answer.missing: No turn or result; it is an action with its rationale.

answer.event: A person of indeterminate sex in Biri was operated on and the covering of his genitals torn open.
answer.turn: Afterwards he fathered seven children.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda's view is defended by suggesting the children were not his.
answer.summary: In the town of Biri there was a tumtum who was placed in a chair and surgically opened, and who went on to father seven children. Rabbi Ami cites this against Rabbi Yehuda, who could answer that the children's paternity should be checked.
answer.missing: The case is only cited as an objection; it is not told as a narrative.

answer.event: Minyamin, a first-generation Egyptian convert, married another first-generation Egyptian convert.
answer.outcome: He planned to marry his son to a second-generation Egyptian convert so that his grandson could enter the congregation.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled his friend Minyamin, an Egyptian convert among Rabbi Akiva's students. Minyamin said he had married a first-generation Egyptian convert and intended to marry his son to a second-generation one, so that his grandson would be permitted to marry into Israel.
answer.missing: It is a reported statement of plans; the outcome is not told.

answer.event: A debtor hid his money by claiming it belonged to a gentile.
answer.turn: Because he acted improperly, the Sages acted harshly with him.
answer.outcome: They forced him to sell his land to pay the creditor.
answer.summary: Asked what really happened in a case attributed to Rava, Rav Hama explained that the debtor had shielded his money by claiming it was a gentile's. Because he behaved dishonestly, the Sages treated him harshly and made him sell his land himself to pay.
answer.missing: The forced sale is supplied partly from context and the translator's gloss.

answer.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yohanan
answer.event: Reish Lakish demanded proof of threshing-floor teruma to confirm a priest, and Rabbi Elazar objected; later the same happened before Rabbi Yohanan, who raised the same objection.
answer.turn: Reish Lakish realized Rabbi Elazar had been quoting Rabbi Yohanan without attribution.
answer.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing bar Nappaha by name.
answer.summary: A man told Reish Lakish someone was a priest because he read first from the Torah; Reish Lakish asked whether he had seen him receive teruma, and Rabbi Elazar retorted that priesthood cannot depend on a threshing floor. Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same exchange happened and Rabbi Yohanan said the very same words. Reish Lakish turned and glared at Rabbi Elazar: you heard this from bar Nappaha and did not tell us in his name?

answer.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain teaching.
answer.turn: Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it, and had even drawn three conclusions from it.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef said he did not know a ruling about side posts. His student Abaye reminded him that he had taught them that very ruling and had derived three laws from it, which Abaye then listed. Rav Yosef's response is not given.
answer.missing: Rav Yosef's reaction; the reason he forgot appears only in the translator's gloss.

answer.actor: Residents of a crooked alley in Sura; Rav Hisda
answer.event: Residents placed a rolled-up mat at the bend of a crooked alley to permit carrying.
answer.turn: Rav Hisda declared it valid by neither Rav nor Shmuel.
answer.outcome: The mat was deemed ineffective because the wind could blow it over.
answer.summary: In Sura, the people of an L-shaped alley rolled up a mat and set it at the bend as a side post. Rav Hisda said this works by no one's opinion, since a mat the wind can knock down counts for nothing.
answer.missing: Most of the passage is legal analysis; the event is a single action.

answer.event: Rabbi Elazar taught that the unlearned will not be resurrected, and Rabbi Yohanan objected that God would not be pleased.
answer.turn: Rabbi Elazar defended his view from another verse, then saw that Rabbi Yohanan was grieved.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Elazar found a remedy: those who support Torah scholars are counted as cleaving to God.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar taught that common, unlearned people will not rise at the resurrection. Rabbi Yohanan protested that God would not be pleased with such a statement, and Rabbi Elazar backed it with another verse. Seeing his teacher distressed, Rabbi Elazar told him he had found them a remedy: whoever marries his daughter to a scholar or supports scholars with his wealth is considered to cleave to the Divine Presence.

answer.actor: A woman selling belts and a man who snatched one
answer.event: A man snatched a belt from a woman selling belts and, when she demanded it back, asked if she would be betrothed to him if he returned it; she took it and stayed silent.
answer.turn: Her silence looked like consent to betrothal.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled she was not betrothed, since she could say she simply took back her own property.
answer.summary: A woman was selling belts when a man grabbed one from her. She told him to give it back, and he asked whether, if he did, she would be betrothed to him. She took the belt and said nothing. Rav Nahman ruled that her silence proved nothing: she could say she was only taking back what was hers.

answer.actor: The daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Guryon
answer.event: The Sages allotted the widowed daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Guryon two se'a of wine a week just for cooking pudding.
answer.turn: She blessed them that they should allot the same to their own daughters, but she was a widow awaiting levirate marriage.
answer.outcome: The Sages did not answer amen to her blessing, not wanting their daughters to share her plight.
answer.summary: After her husband died, the Sages set the support of Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter-in-law at two se'a of wine each week, only for cooking. In gratitude she blessed them: may you allot the same for your own daughters. Because she was a widow waiting on her brother-in-law, the Sages declined to answer amen.

answer.event: During a time of divine anger and famine, the Sages asked Rav Yosef to pray for mercy.
answer.turn: He pointed out that Elisha, who fed 2,200 scholars, did not pray in a time of anger.
answer.outcome: He refused to pray, asking how he could do what Elisha did not.
answer.summary: In Rav Yosef's time there was a famine seen as divine anger. The Sages urged him to pray for mercy. He answered that the prophet Elisha, who supported 2,200 scholars, did not pray in such a time, so how could he? He declined.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a minor girl; Ravina
answer.event: A man betrothed a minor girl in the marketplace with a bundle of vegetables, without her father's consent.
answer.turn: The question was whether the father might have approved the betrothal.
answer.outcome: Ravina ruled there was no concern, since the betrothal was done in a degrading manner.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a young girl in the marketplace using a bundle of vegetables, without her father's approval. Ravina ruled that even those who worry a father may have approved a betrothal would not worry here, because no father would approve such a degrading betrothal. The betrothal was disregarded.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman conditionally, and the Sages
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman on a condition and then had relations with her.
answer.turn: The Sages could not rule the betrothal void.
answer.outcome: The Sages could not let her leave without a bill of divorce.
answer.summary: Rav Kahana, citing Ulla, reports that a man once betrothed a woman conditionally and then lived with her. The Sages did not have the power to release her without a bill of divorce, so a divorce was required.
answer.missing: The details of the incident: who was involved and what the condition was; the report is a bare mention.

answer.event: Levi recited five wedding blessings at the wedding of Rabbi's son, and Rav Asi recited six at the wedding of Rav Ashi's son.
answer.summary: Levi visited Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house during his son Rabbi Shimon's wedding and recited five of the wedding blessings. Rav Asi visited Rav Ashi's house during his son Mar's wedding and recited six.
answer.missing: Any turn or consequence; these are two bare reports of a practice.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef, Abaye, and a daughter seeking support
answer.event: A case came before Rav Yosef, who told the heirs to support the daughter from dates drying on mats.
answer.turn: Abaye objected that not even a creditor may collect from orphans' movable property.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef explained he meant dates still attached to the tree, and defended this again when Abaye pressed.
answer.summary: A case about a daughter's support came before Rav Yosef, who told the dead man's sons to give her dates that were drying on mats. Abaye challenged him: a creditor could not collect that way, so why should she? Rav Yosef clarified that he meant ripe dates still on the tree, and when Abaye pressed again, he said he meant dates that still needed the tree.
answer.missing: Whether the daughter actually received anything; the exchange ends as legal argument.

answer.actor: A betrothed couple and Rav Yosef
answer.event: A betrothed man and his pregnant betrothed came before Rav Yosef; she said the child was his, and he agreed.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled there was nothing to be concerned about, since he admitted it and the law follows Rabban Gamliel in any case.
answer.summary: A betrothed couple came before Rav Yosef because she was pregnant. She said she had conceived from him, and he confirmed it. Rav Yosef ruled there was no cause for concern: the man admitted paternity, and even otherwise her word would be believed.

answer.event: Visiting Neharde'a, Rav Avya saw a man tying a door bolt with a reed.
answer.turn: He judged the reed an inadequate fastening.
answer.outcome: He ruled that the door may not be locked with it on Shabbat.
answer.summary: Rav Avya came to Neharde'a and saw a man fastening a door bolt to the door with a reed. He ruled that this door could not be locked with that bolt on Shabbat, because the reed did not properly attach the bolt.

answer.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his weekly four dinars to a pauper by his wife's hand.
answer.turn: She overheard the household asking whether he would dine on silver or gold tablecloths, and reported he did not need charity.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hanina quoted Rabbi Elazar: we should be grateful to swindlers, since they excuse our failures to the truly poor.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send a poor man four dinars every Friday. One week his wife delivered it and came back saying the man did not need charity: she had heard his household ask whether he would eat on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina responded with Rabbi Elazar's saying that we should appreciate swindlers, for without them we would be sinning daily against the truly poor.

answer.event: A dispute about a child's gift was sent to Rav Mordekhai with its attributions reversed.
answer.turn: Rav Mordekhai recalled asking Rav Ashi, who stood with one foot on the step, and Rav Ashi said a child's gift is valid.
answer.outcome: Rav Mordekhai sent word to Mar bar Rav Ashi reminding him of the incident.
answer.summary: Two sages disagreed whether a young child's gift is valid, and the opinions were reported to Rav Mordekhai with the names swapped. He sent word to Mar bar Rav Ashi: wasn't it so that when your father stood with one foot on the ground and one on the step, we asked him, and he said a child's gift is valid in every case?
answer.missing: How Mar bar Rav Ashi responded to the message.

answer.actor: An Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael
answer.event: An Amorite asked a resident of the Land how many dates the palm on the Jordan bank yields, and was told sixty kor.
answer.turn: The Amorite scoffed that in his people's day it yielded 120, so the newcomers had ruined the land.
answer.outcome: The resident answered that he had spoken of only one side of the tree.
answer.summary: An Amorite asked a man from the Land of Israel how much fruit they harvested from a palm by the Jordan. Sixty kor, the man said. The Amorite mocked him: you have barely arrived and already ruined it, since we used to take 120. The man replied that he was only counting one side of the tree.

answer.actor: Ravina and his host in Mehoza
answer.event: In Mehoza, Ravina's host showed him a slaughtering knife, and Ravina sent him to show it to Rava.
answer.turn: The host asked why, since Rava allows a scholar to check a knife for himself.
answer.outcome: Ravina replied that he was only buying the meat, so it was not slaughter for himself.
answer.summary: Ravina visited Mehoza, Rava's town, and his host showed him a slaughtering knife to check. Ravina told him to take it to Rava. The host asked why, since Rava rules a scholar may check a knife for himself. Ravina answered that he was merely buying meat from the host, so the rule did not apply.

answer.event: Faced with Rav Hamnuna's challenge, Rava fell silent.
answer.turn: After Rav Hamnuna left, Rava thought of an answer, doubted it, and then confirmed it from a baraita.
answer.outcome: He concluded the challenge could be answered as Rabbi Elazar's view.
answer.summary: Rav Hamnuna challenged Rava with a baraita, and Rava had no answer. Once Rav Hamnuna left, Rava reproached himself for not saying the baraita follows Rabbi Elazar. He then doubted whether Rabbi Elazar held so in this kind of case, and finally recalled a baraita showing that he did.
answer.missing: The start of the exchange, Rav Hamnuna's original question and Rava's position, comes before the segments shown.

answer.event: A never-married man told Rav Nahman that he found his bride without signs of virginity.
answer.turn: His claim revealed experience he should not have had.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ordered him flogged, since he must have been with prostitutes.
answer.summary: A man who had never been married came to Rav Nahman and claimed his bride was not a virgin. Rav Nahman ordered him flogged with palm branches: how could an unmarried man know, unless he had been with prostitutes?

answer.event: Rav Ashi came to Rav Kahana's house for a wedding and recited all seven blessings on the first day.
answer.outcome: On later days he recited all of them only if new guests came, and otherwise only two.
answer.summary: Rav Ashi attended a wedding at Rav Kahana's house. On the first day he recited all seven wedding blessings. On the following days he recited them all only when new guests were present; otherwise he treated it as a continuation and said just two blessings.
answer.missing: Any turn; the passage describes his practice over the days rather than an event that changes.

answer.actor: A man who betrothed a woman in her waiting period, and Rafram
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman within three months of her divorce or widowhood and then fled.
answer.outcome: Rafram ruled that his flight was punishment enough, and he was not excommunicated.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman during the three-month waiting period after her previous marriage ended, and then ran away. When the case came up, Rafram ruled that his running away was sufficient and no further penalty was needed.
answer.missing: Details of the actual incident; it is a bare report attached to a stated dispute.

answer.actor: A herdsman of orphans' cattle, a creditor, and Rav Nahman
answer.event: A creditor seized an ox from a herdsman tending orphans' cattle; the creditor said he took it while the debtor lived, the herdsman said after his death.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman asked if the herdsman had witnesses to the seizure, and he had none.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the creditor, who could have claimed he bought the ox.
answer.summary: A creditor took an ox from a herdsman caring for orphans' cattle. The creditor claimed he took it while their father was alive; the herdsman said it was after his death. Before Rav Nahman, the herdsman admitted he had no witnesses to the seizure, so Rav Nahman ruled that the creditor was believed, since he could even have claimed he had bought it.

answer.event: A woman named Me'oret made her slave do three of the dangerous acts.
answer.outcome: The slave died.
answer.summary: A woman named Me'oret made her slave perform three of the acts said to be deadly together, and he died. The Gemara explains that he was weak.
answer.missing: Any detail of the event; it is a bare report cited in a legal discussion.

answer.event: People asked Rabbi Elai where Rabbi Abbahu was hiding.
answer.turn: Rabbi Elai answered in a riddle: Abbahu had consulted the Nasi and gone south to the Sages there.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abbahu had disappeared, and people asked Rabbi Elai to show them where he was hiding. Rabbi Elai answered cryptically that Abbahu had taken counsel with 'the one who crowns' (the Nasi) and had gone south to 'Mephibosheth', meaning the Sages of the south.
answer.missing: Why Abbahu was hiding and what came of it are not told; the exchange is only a clever reply.

answer.event: Rav arrived at Apsetaya and forbade climbing even a stripped tree on Shabbat.
answer.turn: The Gemara explains he did it not because it was prohibited but because the place was lax and needed a fence.
answer.summary: Rav came to a place called Apsetaya and forbade its residents to climb even a tree already stripped of its branches on Shabbat. The Gemara explains that this was not the strict law: Rav found a place where transgression was common and added a safeguard.
answer.missing: Only a bare report of a ruling; no reaction or consequence is told.

answer.actor: Ameimar, a woman seeking a tenth of her father's estate, and her brothers
answer.event: A woman came before Ameimar demanding a tenth of her father's estate as her dowry share.
answer.turn: Her brothers said they would pay her off in cash if they had the money, and Ameimar, who had held a daughter is an heir, said nothing against it.
answer.outcome: Rav Minyumi, who witnessed it, concluded Ameimar had retracted and now treated her as a creditor.
answer.summary: Rav Minyumi was standing before Ameimar when a woman came asking for a tenth of her father's estate. Her brothers told her that if they had the money they would pay her off in cash, and Ameimar stayed silent. From his silence Rav Minyumi understood that Ameimar had abandoned his view that a daughter inherits, and now treated her as a creditor who can be paid in money.

answer.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions taken from the field he worked.
answer.turn: Rava asked him who had given him the onions, meaning they were stolen.
answer.outcome: The betrothal was invalid.
answer.summary: A sharecropper betrothed a woman using a handful of onions from the field he worked and then asked Rava whether she was betrothed. Rava asked him who had given him permission to take them: they were stolen, so the betrothal failed. The Gemara adds that had he taken a whole bundle, he could have claimed it as his share of the crop.

answer.actor: A fox and the people who weighed a turnip
answer.event: A fox made its nest inside a turnip.
answer.turn: When the turnip was weighed, it still came to sixty litra by the Tzippori measure.
answer.summary: To show that future wheat kernels as large as an ox's kidneys are not unbelievable, the Sages cite an incident: a fox nested inside a turnip, and when people weighed the hollowed turnip it still weighed sixty litra by the measure of Tzippori.
answer.missing: It is a cited marvel rather than a full story; no one's situation changes.

answer.event: Ravina, holding wine belonging to his orphaned nephew, was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell.
answer.turn: He asked Rav Ashi whether he could take the orphan's wine along with his own.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi told him to go, since the orphan's wine is no better than his own.
answer.summary: Ravina was looking after wine belonging to his orphaned nephew, Ravina the younger, and was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell. He asked Rav Ashi whether he could take the orphan's wine with him. Rav Ashi told him to go ahead: if this was good enough for his own wine, it was good enough for the orphan's.

answer.actor: A man who conditioned a bill of divorce
answer.event: A man told witnesses that if he did not marry his betrothed by the New Moon of Adar, the document would be a bill of divorce.
answer.turn: When Adar came, he claimed he had said Nisan.
answer.summary: A man told witnesses that if he did not marry his betrothed by the New Moon of Adar, a bill of divorce would take effect. When the date arrived he claimed he had actually said Nisan. The Gemara then weighs the legal concerns without saying how the case was decided.
answer.missing: The ruling or outcome of the case is not stated.

answer.actor: The Sages examining a found bill of divorce
answer.event: A bill of divorce was found in Sura in the name of Anan bar Hiyya of Neharde'a.
answer.turn: The Sages found only one other man of that name, and witnesses said he was in Neharde'a the day it was written.
answer.summary: A bill of divorce was found in Sura, written by 'Anan bar Hiyya of Neharde'a'. The Sages searched all the way from Sura to Neharde'a and found only one other man with that name, Anan bar Hiyya of Hagra, and witnesses testified he had been with them in Neharde'a that day. Abaye and Rava then argue over whether to worry about him, but no decision about the woman is told.
answer.missing: What was done with the bill of divorce is not stated; the rest is legal argument.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Shumni and Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya
answer.event: Two scholars parting at the ford of the Yofti River agreed each would say a teaching the other had not heard.
answer.outcome: Each one offered a teaching: one defined tipsy vs drunk, the other how to keep a convert's property.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abba bar Shumni and Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya were taking leave of each other at the ford of the Yofti River. Following the advice to part with a word of halakha, they agreed each would say something new to the other. One explained the difference between someone who has drunk and someone who is drunk; the other taught that one who takes a convert's property should buy a Torah scroll with it.
answer.missing: The frame is a narrative but nothing turns; it serves to deliver teachings.

answer.event: Rav Hisda's daughter asked her father, who studied through the nights, whether he wanted to sleep a little.
answer.turn: He replied that long days of no opportunity are coming, and then he will sleep plenty.
answer.outcome: He kept studying, implying he would rest only in death.
answer.summary: Rav Hisda used to spend his nights studying. His daughter asked him whether he did not want to sleep a little. He answered that long days, short in chances to study and do mitzvot, would soon come, and then he would sleep a great deal, meaning after his death.

answer.event: A dying Madonite wanted to give away much movable property as a gift.
answer.turn: The Sages told him it could only be done through land, so he bought a small rocky plot and gave the goods along with portions of it.
answer.outcome: He died, and the Sages carried out his instructions.
answer.summary: A Madonite in Jerusalem, ill and short of time, had many movable goods he wanted to give away. The Sages told him the only way was to transfer them together with land. He bought a plot near Jerusalem and declared that its northern part, along with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, went to a certain person. He died, and the Sages honoured what he had said.

answer.actor: The returning exiles and their prophets
answer.event: The exiles returning from Babylonia camped at the Heker well.
answer.turn: The prophets among them permitted them to draw from it on a Festival, following an ancestral custom.
answer.summary: When the exiles came back from Babylonia they camped by a particular Heker well, and the prophets among them allowed them to draw water from it on a Festival. The text clarifies that the prophets were really confirming a custom passed down from their forefathers.
answer.missing: Little more than a report of a permission; no development or consequence.

answer.actor: The people of Neharde'a and Rav Nahman
answer.event: During a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat.
answer.turn: Then wheat arrived and the sales proved unnecessary.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions go back to their owners.
answer.summary: A drought struck Neharde'a and everyone sold their mansions to buy food. Soon afterwards a shipment of wheat arrived, making the sales pointless. Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions must be returned to their original owners.

answer.actor: Mar Yehuda, Rav Yosef, Rav Shmuel son of Rabba bar bar Hana, and Rabba
answer.event: Mar Yehuda found two scholars at the door of Rabba's study hall and challenged them with a contradiction about Rabbi Shimon's view.
answer.turn: They were silent and had no answer, so they went to Rabba.
answer.outcome: Rabba said a quarrelsome person had put them up to it and resolved the contradiction.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda came upon Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel standing at the entrance of Rabba's study hall and posed them a contradiction between two teachings of Rabbi Shimon about animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard. They had no answer and fell silent. They took the question to Rabba, who remarked that a quarrelsome man had set them up, and then explained that the first teaching dealt with an animal found to be a tereifa.

answer.event: Rabbi Zeira was avoiding his teacher Rav Yehuda because he wanted to move to Eretz Yisrael.
answer.turn: Rav Yehuda held that leaving Babylonia for the Land violates a commandment.
answer.summary: Rabbi Zeira wanted to go up to the Land of Israel, so he kept out of sight of his teacher Rav Yehuda, who taught that anyone leaving Babylonia for Israel transgresses a positive commandment.
answer.missing: Whether Rabbi Zeira went and what happened next are not in the segments shown; [3] gives only the verse and Rabbi Zeira's reading of it.

answer.actor: A man who sold his mother's marriage contract, Rami bar Hama and Rava
answer.event: A man sold his expected rights to his mother's marriage contract, saying he would not refund if his mother objected.
answer.turn: His mother died without objecting, and he himself then contested the sale.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled against him: he had guaranteed the sale against his own objections even if not his mother's.
answer.summary: A man sold, for a small sum, his future right to collect his mother's marriage contract, telling the buyer he would not refund the money if his mother objected. His mother died without objecting, and then he himself challenged the sale. Rami bar Hama thought he stood in his mother's place, but Rava ruled that he had certainly guaranteed the sale against his own objections, so the sale stood.

answer.event: Rabbi Abbahu moved an oil lamp on Shabbat in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's town but refrained from doing so in Rabbi Yohanan's town.
answer.turn: His inconsistent behavior is explained as deference to Rabbi Yohanan in his own locale, and his servant, who might be confused, had to be told why.
answer.outcome: He informed his servant of the reason for the change in behavior.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abbahu, who held it permitted to move a burnt-out oil lamp on Shabbat, did so when visiting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's town. When he visited Rabbi Yohanan's town, where it was forbidden, he refrained out of respect for Rabbi Yohanan. To keep his servant from drawing the wrong conclusion, he explained to him why he acted differently there.
answer.missing: This is a recurring habit rather than a single event; the servant explanation is the Gemara's resolution, not a narrated scene.

answer.event: Rav arrived at the house of the son of a vinegar strainer and examined the family.
answer.turn: The examination was of whether they fell silent in quarrels, not of their genealogy.
answer.summary: Rav once came to the household of a vinegar strainer's son and had its members examined. According to the Gemara, he told the examiners to check whether the family members fell silent when they quarreled, a sign of good lineage.
answer.missing: The result of the examination and any consequence for the family are not given.

answer.event: In an actual case, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave an orphan girl one-twelfth of her late father's property as her dowry.
answer.outcome: She received one-twelfth rather than the standard one-tenth.
answer.summary: Rav Adda bar Ahava reported that in one case Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi awarded an orphaned daughter one-twelfth of her father's estate for her dowry. The Gemara explains that the father's wishes had been assessed in that case.
answer.missing: The details of the case and the parties are not given; it is reported only as a ruling.

answer.actor: An Arab and his camel, as witnessed by Rabba bar bar Hanna
answer.event: Rabba bar bar Hanna saw an Arab take his sword and cut open his camel.
answer.turn: The camel died so fast that it did not even finish braying.
answer.outcome: The camel died instantly; Abaye later explained it was emaciated.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Hanna recounted that he once saw an Arab slash open his camel with a sword. The camel died so quickly that it had not stopped braying. Abaye explained that the camel must have been weak and emaciated.

answer.actor: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
answer.event: The widow came before Rav Yosef and asked him to allot her sustenance, wine, and then silk garments.
answer.turn: When he asked why she needed silk, she retorted that it was for him and his colleagues.
answer.outcome: Her answer stands as the last word: she should not be shamed before the scholars.
answer.summary: A widow came before Rav Yosef and asked him to allocate support for her from her late husband's estate. He granted her food and wine. When she also demanded silk garments and he asked why, she answered that it was for him, his friends and his friends' friends, meaning she should not appear shabby before the sages.
answer.missing: Whether he granted the silk is not stated.

answer.event: The Sages asked Rabbi Abbahu where Rabbi Elai was hiding.
answer.turn: Rabbi Abbahu answered with a cryptic, punning riddle.
answer.outcome: His answer implied Rabbi Elai was asleep after a night kept awake by a lively young woman.
answer.summary: The Sages, unable to find Rabbi Elai, asked Rabbi Abbahu where he was. Rabbi Abbahu replied with a riddle full of wordplay: Rabbi Elai had rejoiced with a lively young woman of priestly descent who kept him awake. The point is that Rabbi Elai was sleeping.
answer.missing: It is an exchange with a witty answer; there is no further event or resolution.

answer.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
answer.event: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna were about to permit a nursing mother to remarry immediately, following a baraita.
answer.turn: An old woman told them Rav Nahman had forbidden it in her own case, and Rav Pappi reminded them of a baraita and a ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's decrees.
answer.outcome: They admitted they had forgotten the principle.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua were about to rule, based on a baraita, that a woman who had handed her baby to a wet nurse could remarry right away. An old woman stopped them, saying that Rav Nahman had forbidden exactly this in her case. Rav Pappi then pointed out a baraita requiring all women to wait three months, and Shmuel's rule that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's decrees. The two sages admitted they had not had this in mind.

answer.event: A case came before Rabbi Yitzhak in Antioch.
answer.outcome: He ruled that collection by oath in the husband's absence applies only to a marriage contract, not to a creditor.
answer.summary: Rav Aha Sar HaBira reported that a case came before Rabbi Yitzhak in Antioch. Rabbi Yitzhak ruled that a woman may collect her marriage contract with an oath in her husband's absence, but a creditor may not collect a debt that way.
answer.missing: The facts of the case itself are not given; only the ruling is reported.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elai, Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi and Rabbi Shimon bar Abba
answer.event: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed by two sages who were studying, and they stood up for him.
answer.turn: He told them they should not have stood: they were ordained and he was not, and the Torah does not rise before its students.
answer.outcome: He rebuked their gesture of respect as unnecessary.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi were sitting and studying when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba walked by, and they rose for him. He told them there was no need: they were ordained scholars while he was only an associate, and in any case people engaged in Torah study need not stand before those who study it.

answer.actor: A man from Eretz Yisrael and Rabbi Hanina
answer.event: A man whose brother had died leaving a widow in Bei Hoza'a in Babylonia asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go down to perform levirate marriage.
answer.turn: Rabbi Hanina condemned the dead brother for leaving the land and marrying abroad, blessing God for killing him.
answer.outcome: He told the man not to follow his brother out of Eretz Yisrael.
answer.summary: A man in Eretz Yisrael learned that his childless brother had died, leaving a widow in distant Bei Hoza'a whom he was obligated to marry or release. He asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could travel to Babylonia to marry her. Rabbi Hanina replied harshly that the brother had married a foreign woman and died, blessed be God who killed him, and asked whether the man now wanted to go down after him.

answer.actor: A woman litigant, Rav Beivai bar Abaye and Rav Pappi
answer.event: A woman obliged to take an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court asked for a document of rights in advance before agreeing to swear in town.
answer.turn: Rav Beivai ordered the document written for her before the oath.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappi mocked the ruling, saying Rav Beivai spoke unfortunate words because he came from an unfortunate family.
answer.summary: A woman was required to take an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court, and her opponent asked that she swear publicly in town, hoping shame would make her confess. She agreed only if the court first wrote her a document of rights that would be handed over once she swore. Rav Beivai told the scribes to write it. Rav Pappi sharply criticized the decision, jibing that Rav Beivai's descent from an ill-fated family led him to say ill-fated things.

answer.event: Villagers asked Rabbi Yirmeya whether one may make an eiruv with moist beans, and he did not know.
answer.turn: Back at the study hall he was told Rabbi Yannai's ruling.
answer.outcome: He learned that moist beans are permitted, in the amount of a handful.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yirmeya once visited some villages, where the people asked him whether an eiruv could be made with moist beans. He did not know the answer. When he returned to the study hall, his colleagues told him that Rabbi Yannai permitted it, and Rav Yehiel specified a handful as the amount.

answer.actor: The judges of Neharde'a, Rav Hana bar Bizna and Rav Nahman
answer.event: Judges in Neharde'a and Rav Hana bar Bizna in Pumbedita ruled that daughters be supported from movable property.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman ordered them to reverse their rulings or he would seize their houses.
answer.summary: In Neharde'a the local judges, and in Pumbedita Rav Hana bar Bizna, ruled that orphan daughters must be supported from their father's movable property, and collected accordingly. Rav Nahman told them to undo their decisions, threatening to take their own houses to compensate the heirs otherwise.
answer.missing: Whether the judges complied is not stated.

answer.event: Judges ruled a case according to Rabbi Tarfon, and Reish Lakish overturned their ruling.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan criticized Reish Lakish for reversing it.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan told him he had treated the matter as if it were Torah law.
answer.summary: Some judges decided an inheritance case following Rabbi Tarfon's view, and Reish Lakish reversed their decision and returned the money to the heirs. Rabbi Yohanan rebuked him, saying he had acted as though it were a matter of Torah law that must be corrected.

answer.event: A woman whose husband could not father children demanded her marriage contract from Rabbi Ami.
answer.turn: When he said she was not commanded to have children, she asked who would care for her in old age.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled that in such a case the husband is forced to divorce her and pay.
answer.summary: A woman came before Rabbi Ami asking for a divorce and her marriage contract payment because her husband could not give her children. He told her to go away, since women are not commanded to have children. She answered by asking what would become of her in old age. Rabbi Ami then ruled that in such a case the husband is compelled to divorce her.

answer.event: A son-in-law passed by the entrance of his father-in-law's house, and Rav Sheshet had him flogged.
answer.turn: There were rumors about him and his mother-in-law.
answer.outcome: He was flogged.
answer.summary: A man walked past the door of his father-in-law's house, and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. The reason was that rumors already linked him to his mother-in-law, and walking by fed them.
answer.missing: It is a bare report cited in a legal discussion; the rumors explanation is the Gemara's.

answer.event: Rabbi went to study Torah with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua.
answer.turn: The students ganged up on him like fighting roosters and did not let him learn.
