answer.outcome: He managed to learn only one teaching from the mishna.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalled going to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua. The other students banded together against him like aggressive roosters and would not let him learn. He came away with just one teaching: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling about a hermaphrodite.

answer.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
answer.event: The Sages allotted Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter four hundred gold coins for perfumes for a single day.
answer.turn: Instead of complaining she blessed them, or perhaps mocked them, saying they should pledge the same for their own daughters.
answer.outcome: The Sages answered Amen.
answer.summary: When the Sages set aside four hundred gold coins from her late husband's estate for the perfume expenses of Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter for one day, she told them to allot the same for their own daughters. The Sages responded Amen.

answer.actor: Rav Anan bar Tahalifa and Rav Ashi
answer.event: Each stood before his teacher when a strong-smelling dish was brought, and the teacher shared it.
answer.turn: Without being given some, each would have been endangered by craving.
answer.outcome: They were given some and were not harmed.
answer.summary: Rav Anan bar Tahalifa recalled standing before Mar Shmuel when a mushroom dish was brought; had Shmuel not given him some, his craving would have endangered him. Rav Ashi told the same about turnip slices in vinegar served to Rav Kahana.
answer.missing: These are brief first-person anecdotes used as evidence; they have little narrative development.

answer.actor: The father of Shmuel and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
answer.event: A bill of divorce signed by one Androlinai of Neharde'a was found, and Shmuel's father sent the question of its validity to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia.
answer.turn: No one knew whether the Androlinai named was the husband or another man of the same name.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia replied that all of Neharde'a must be searched for another man of that name.
answer.summary: A bill of divorce turned up in Neharde'a, written by a man named Androlinai divorcing his wife. Because it was unclear whether it was really her husband or someone else with the same name, Shmuel's father sent the question to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia in the Land of Israel. He answered that the whole city of Neharde'a should be checked for another Androlinai.

answer.actor: Mar Zutra and a rebellious wife
answer.event: A wife refused her husband, saying he disgusted her, and Mar Zutra compelled her to stay with him.
answer.turn: Despite the coercion, the couple's union produced a great sage.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hanina of Sura was born to them, though the Gemara attributes this to heavenly help rather than a precedent.
answer.summary: A woman rebelled against her husband, claiming she found him repulsive, and Mar Zutra forced her to remain married to him. From that couple came Rabbi Hanina of Sura. The Gemara adds that this good result came only through heavenly assistance and should not be taken as proof that such coercion is good.

answer.event: A crooked alleyway in Neharde'a was required to have doors, by applying both Rav's and Shmuel's stringencies.
answer.outcome: The alleyway was required to have doors.
answer.summary: In Neharde'a there was an L-shaped alleyway, and the authorities required it to have doors, combining a stringency of Rav with one of Shmuel. The rest of the passage is legal analysis of why both stringencies apply.
answer.missing: Who made the ruling and any consequence beyond the ruling itself.

answer.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his weekly four dinars to a pauper through his wife, who came back saying the man did not need charity.
answer.turn: She had overheard the household asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths, revealing he was wealthy.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Hanina responded by citing Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers, since they excuse our failure to give enough to the truly poor.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send four dinars to a poor man every Friday. One week his wife delivered it and returned saying the man did not need it: she had overheard his household asking whether he would dine on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina did not grow bitter; he quoted Rabbi Elazar that swindlers should be appreciated, because without them we would be guilty every day of neglecting the real poor.

answer.event: Ulla, who often traveled to the Land of Israel, died outside it, and Rabbi Elazar was told.
answer.turn: Rabbi Elazar lamented that Ulla died in an unclean land; told that his coffin was being brought to Israel, he was not consoled.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Elazar said that being received by the land in life is not like being received after death.
answer.summary: Ulla regularly went up to the Land of Israel, but he died abroad. When Rabbi Elazar heard, he mourned him with the verse about dying in an unclean land. People told him Ulla's coffin was coming for burial in Israel, but he replied that being absorbed by the land after death is not the same as being absorbed while alive.

answer.actor: A dying man, his heirs and his daughter
answer.event: A man bequeathed a palm tree to his daughter but left only two half-shares of palm trees.
answer.turn: The heirs wanted to give her the two halves, raising the question of whether two halves count as a palm tree.
answer.outcome: Rav Mordekhai cited Rava that people do call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs could give her the halves.
answer.summary: A man's will left a palm tree to his daughter, but when he died the estate held only two half-shares of palm trees owned with partners. The heirs wanted to give her those two halves. Rav Ashi wondered whether that fulfilled the father's words, and Rav Mordekhai reported in Rava's name that people do speak of two halves as a palm tree, so the heirs' offer stood.

answer.event: Rabbi ruled in a case according to Rabbi Elazar's opinion.
answer.turn: He afterwards remembered something about that ruling.
answer.outcome: He said Rabbi Elazar is worthy of reliance in exigent circumstances.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once ruled in accordance with Rabbi Elazar. Afterward he recalled that his ruling was questionable, and said that Rabbi Elazar is a worthy authority to rely on in a time of pressing need.
answer.missing: The details of the case he ruled on, and what exactly he remembered.

answer.event: Mar Yehuda found the residents of Mavrakhta placing their eiruv in a synagogue and told them to put it farther in to gain more distance.
answer.turn: Rava rebuked him, calling him argumentative.
answer.outcome: Rava declared that no one follows Rabbi Akiva's view on this in eiruv law, so the placement made no difference.
answer.summary: Mar Yehuda came upon the people of Mavrakhta placing their eiruv in the synagogue of Beit Agovar and advised them to set it farther inside so they could walk farther on Shabbat. Rava scolded him as a contrarian, saying that in eiruv matters nobody follows the opinion of Rabbi Akiva that his advice relied on.

answer.actor: Rava and one of the Sages
answer.event: Rava boasted that he was like ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias, ready for any question.
answer.turn: A Sage asked how many apples are needed for an eiruv; Rava answered that apples cannot be used, and the Sage challenged him from a mishna.
answer.summary: In high spirits, Rava declared himself as sharp as ben Azzai and ready to answer anything. A scholar promptly asked him how many apples are needed for an eiruv. Rava retorted that apples are not used for an eiruv, but the scholar cited a mishna implying that all foods combine for an eiruv.
answer.missing: How the exchange ends, i.e., Rava's response to the challenge.

answer.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
answer.event: They bought a maidservant for copper coins but, lacking the money, left a piece of silver as collateral.
answer.turn: The price of the maidservant rose and the sellers wanted to back out.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled that neither coins nor collateral had effected the sale, so it was void.
answer.summary: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin agreed to buy a maidservant for copper coins, but since they did not have the coins they deposited a piece of silver as security. When her price went up, the sellers wanted to cancel. Rabbi Ami ruled that no payment and no valid collateral had changed hands, so there was no sale.

answer.event: Seven teachings said on Shabbat morning before Rav Hisda in Sura were repeated before Rava in Pumbedita at the end of that Shabbat.
answer.turn: The distance was too great to travel on Shabbat, raising who carried them.
answer.summary: Seven teachings were said one Shabbat morning before Rav Hisda in Sura and were heard again before Rava in Pumbedita late that same Shabbat, though the distance could not be walked on Shabbat. The passage cites this only as evidence; who brought them is debated afterwards as a legal point.
answer.missing: Who carried the teachings and how; the passage only gestures at the incident.

answer.actor: Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zerika
answer.event: Rabbi Ami was asked whether a master may take payment for a slave who ran off to a foreign army; Rabbi Yirmeya sent Rabbi Zerika to search the sources.
answer.turn: Rabbi Zerika found a baraita about a house seized by a gentile that supplied an answer.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami sent out a ruling to all Israel that the master may take the slave's value and register it in gentile courts.
answer.summary: Rabbi Ami was asked about a slave who fled and joined a foreign army beyond his master's reach: could the master accept the slave's price? Rabbi Yirmeya told Rabbi Zerika to check his sources, and he found a teaching permitting a Jew to take payment for a house a gentile seized by force. Rabbi Ami then issued a public ruling that the master may take the slave's value, since he is like one rescuing money from their hands.
answer.missing: The passage is mainly a legal inquiry; there is little narrative beyond the question, search and ruling.

answer.actor: A man who gave a conditional divorce
answer.event: A man said his bill of divorce would take effect if he did not return within thirty days, and he came back just at the end.
answer.turn: The ferry was on the far side of the river, so he could not cross in time and shouted, 'See that I have come.'
answer.outcome: Shmuel ruled that this did not count as returning.
answer.summary: A man gave agents a bill of divorce, saying it should take effect if he had not returned within thirty days. He arrived at the river at the last moment but the ferry was on the other side, and he could only call across, 'See, I have come!' Shmuel ruled that this was not a return, so the condition was fulfilled.

answer.event: Rava asked Rav Nahman which tanna rejects retroactive designation even for rabbinic laws, citing a baraita.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman was silent and gave no answer.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman said nothing, since he did not accept the version of the school of Ayo that could have answered.
answer.summary: Rava challenged Rav Nahman to identify the tanna behind a teaching that rejects retroactive designation even in rabbinic matters. Rav Nahman fell silent and said nothing at all. The Gemara explains he could have cited the school of Ayo but did not accept that tradition.
answer.missing: This is mostly a scholarly exchange; the only event is the question and the silence.

answer.event: Rav Dimi was stumped by a challenge, and Abaye suggested the answer from a verse.
answer.turn: Abaye's answer matched Rabbi Yohanan's own teaching.
answer.outcome: Rav Dimi praised Abaye as though he had been present when Rabbi Yohanan taught it.
answer.summary: Rav Dimi, faced with a difficulty about a teaching of Rabbi Yohanan, fell silent. Abaye proposed that the case was different because the verse ties the matter to birth. Rav Dimi praised him, saying he had seen Abaye's head among the pillars when Rabbi Yohanan taught it, meaning Abaye understood it as if he had been there.
answer.missing: The start of the exchange (the challenge Rav Dimi faced) is only partly reconstructed from the preceding legal argument.

answer.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
answer.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba met Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying a child to the synagogue to study with only a cheap covering on his head.
answer.turn: Asked why the haste, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cited the verse linking teaching one's children with standing at Sinai.
answer.outcome: From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat breakfast before teaching his child.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing a child to the synagogue to learn, a cheap cloth thrown over his head. When asked what the hurry was, he answered that Scripture places teaching one's descendants right next to standing before God at Sinai. Taking this to heart, Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba never again ate breakfast until he had reviewed and advanced his child's lessons.

answer.event: An incident occurred in Rav Hisda's study hall and was brought to Rav Huna's study hall.
answer.outcome: They resolved it from a mishna about an agent and consecrated property.
answer.summary: Some case arose in Rav Hisda's study hall, and Rav Hisda took it to Rav Huna's study hall, where it was decided on the basis of a mishna about unspoken intentions. The rest is legal reasoning.
answer.missing: What the incident actually was; the passage only mentions that one happened.

answer.actor: A blind man who studied with Mar Shmuel
answer.event: The blind man was late, Mar Shmuel sent a messenger who missed him on the road, and the messenger reported that he saw the man's wife committing adultery.
answer.turn: On a single witness's word, the blind man had to decide whether to divorce his wife.
answer.outcome: Mar Shmuel told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not otherwise.
answer.summary: A blind man used to recite mishnayot before Mar Shmuel. One day he was late, so Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to fetch him; they took different routes and missed each other, and the messenger ended up at the blind man's house. He returned claiming he had seen the man's wife commit adultery. Mar Shmuel told the blind man to divorce her if he believed the messenger, and otherwise not to.

answer.event: Rabbi Akiva picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and separated two tithes from it.
answer.turn: He tithed it according to both Beit Shammai's and Beit Hillel's new-year dates.
answer.summary: Rabbi Akiva once picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and separated from it two different tithes, one according to Beit Shammai, who count that day as the new year for trees, and one according to Beit Hillel, who count the fifteenth. It is a single act cited as evidence, without a real turn or consequence.
answer.missing: Any consequence of his act; it is a brief precedent rather than a full story.

answer.event: Throughout Rav Huna's lifetime, Rav Hisda was asked whether an egg may be cooked in kutah and refused to rule.
answer.outcome: He never issued the ruling while his teacher lived.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef told Abaye that during all the years Rav Huna was alive, his disciple Rav Hisda would not even answer a simple question about cooking an egg in a dairy dish, out of deference to his teacher's authority. It is cited as precedent rather than told as a single episode.
answer.missing: A specific occasion; this reads as a standing practice rather than one event with a turn.

answer.event: A bill of divorce dated by the years of the governor of Bascar came up, and Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda sent the question to Rabba.
answer.turn: Rabba answered that even Rabbi Meir, who is strict about dating, would accept it, because the governor belongs to the ruling kingdom.
answer.outcome: The bill of divorce was ruled valid.
answer.summary: A bill of divorce turned up whose date was written by the years of the governor of Bascar rather than the king. Unsure whether it was valid, Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda sent the case to Rabba. Rabba replied that even Rabbi Meir would accept it, since the governor is an official of the same kingdom, and the document stood.

answer.event: While Rabbi Yehuda and others sat before Rabbi Tarfon, a yevama came to perform halitza.
answer.turn: Rabbi Tarfon told all those present to call out 'He who had his shoe removed' three times.
answer.outcome: The students joined in the declaration at the ceremony.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled that once, while he and others were sitting before Rabbi Tarfon, a widow came to perform the halitza ceremony. Rabbi Tarfon instructed everyone present, not just the judges, to call out three times 'He who had his shoe removed.'
answer.missing: The text does not state explicitly that they did so, only the instruction.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages
answer.event: In Rabbi's days the Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites to marry into the community.
answer.turn: Rabbi objected that even if they could release the people's share, no one could release the altar's share.
answer.outcome: The attempt was blocked.
answer.summary: In the time of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Sages wanted to lift the ban on the Gibeonites and let them marry fellow Jews. Rabbi stopped them: the court might waive the nation's claim on them, but who could waive the claim of the altar they had been assigned to serve?
answer.missing: The outcome is implied by Rabbi's objection, not stated.

answer.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil; Shmuel
answer.event: Rav Yosef issued a practical ruling following Rav's opinion on a father's betrothal of his daughter.
answer.turn: Shmuel took offense and sarcastically asked whether wisdom had been measured out to this man in a larger measure than everyone else.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef of Dabil decided an actual case according to Rav's view, against Shmuel's. Shmuel was offended and mocked him, asking whether he alone had been given a bigger portion of wisdom than everyone else. The incident is cited inside a legal argument about whether Rav and Shmuel truly disagreed.
answer.missing: The details of the case and any consequence of Shmuel's rebuke.

answer.event: Rav saw his uncle Rabbi Hiyya conduct halitza with a laced sandal.
answer.outcome: Because of that, Rav did not limit himself to the tighter Arab sandal.
answer.summary: Rav said that had he not seen his uncle Rabbi Hiyya conduct a halitza ceremony using a laced sandal, he would only ever have used the tight-fitting sandal of the Arabs. The sighting shaped his own practice.
answer.missing: It is a recollection supporting a ruling rather than an episode with its own turn.

answer.actor: Rabbi Elazar and an elder of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's court
answer.event: Rabbi Elazar asked an elder who had been present at a case whether the court had let a woman remarry immediately or only after twelve months.
answer.summary: Rabbi Elazar asked an old man who had sat on Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's court about a past case of a conditional divorce: when they allowed the widow to remarry, was it right away or only after the twelve months of the condition had passed? The text gives only the question.
answer.missing: The original case and the elder's answer.

answer.event: Levi publicly taught Rabbi's ruling that a bill of divorce written on forbidden-benefit items is valid, in Rabbi's name.
answer.turn: The audience did not praise him; when he taught it as the majority's view, they praised him.
answer.outcome: The ruling was received, showing the halakha follows it.
answer.summary: Levi went out and taught that a divorce document written on material one may not benefit from is valid, citing Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. The listeners were unimpressed. He taught it again as the view of the majority, and this time they praised him.

answer.actor: A debtor, his creditor, and a purchaser
answer.event: A man owing 100 dinars sold two plots for 50 each; the creditor seized one and came to seize the other.
answer.turn: The purchaser brought 100 dinars and told the creditor to either accept the plot as worth 100 or take the cash and give up both plots.
answer.summary: A man owed a creditor 100 dinars and sold his two small fields for 50 each. The creditor took one field from the buyer, then came back for the second. The buyer showed up with 100 dinars and offered: count the field as worth 100, or take this money and leave me both fields.
answer.missing: The creditor's response or the court's ruling; only later legal discussion follows.

answer.actor: Two men slurred as children of Arameans; Rav Asi; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
answer.event: People called one man 'son of the Aramean woman' and another 'son of an Aramean man', doubting their parents' conversions.
answer.turn: Rav Asi and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi each pointed out that the parent had immersed for ritual purity, which counts as conversion.
answer.outcome: The men's lineage was upheld.
answer.summary: A man was taunted as the son of an Aramean woman, implying his mother's conversion was invalid; Rav Asi answered that she had surely immersed after menstruation, which suffices. In a similar case, a man called the son of an Aramean man was defended by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who noted that his father had immersed after a seminal emission.
answer.missing: The outcome is implied by the rulings rather than narrated.

answer.actor: The Sages, Rav, Shmuel and Karna
answer.event: Faced with Shmuel's ruling that a minor betrothed without her father's consent needs both divorce and refusal, and Karna's objection, the Sages sent the question to Rav with the two names swapped.
answer.turn: Rav, thinking Shmuel held the lenient view, swore by God that she needs both and that Shmuel could never say otherwise.
answer.outcome: Rav's oath unwittingly confirmed Shmuel's actual ruling.
answer.summary: Shmuel ruled that a girl betrothed without her father's consent needs both a divorce and a refusal; Karna called this self-contradictory. The Sages took the question to Rav but switched whose opinion was whose. Rav swore that she needs both, and that God forbid Shmuel should say anything else, so he ended up backing Shmuel's real position.

answer.actor: A son sent by his father
answer.event: A father told his son to climb a building and bring him chicks; the son sent away the mother bird and took the young.
answer.turn: On the way down he fell and died, despite performing two mitzvot promised long life.
answer.outcome: He died, and the rabbis concluded the promised reward refers to the World-to-Come.
answer.summary: A father asked his son to climb up and fetch him some chicks. The son climbed, sent off the mother bird as the Torah requires, and took the young, keeping both commandments that promise long life. Coming down, he fell and was killed, which led Rabbi Ya'akov to teach that their reward is paid in the next world.

answer.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva
answer.event: The four Sages were sailing from Pelandarsin when their boat set out to sea on Shabbat.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar walked the whole boat, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva would not move beyond four cubits.
answer.outcome: The two pairs held to different practices for the voyage, the latter by choosing strictness.
answer.summary: Four great Sages were returning from Pelandarsin when their ship sailed out on Shabbat, carrying them past their permitted boundary. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya walked freely about the ship. Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva stayed within four cubits, choosing to be strict with themselves.

answer.actor: Rav Aha son of Rav Avya
answer.event: Rav Aha met Rav Ashi's students and asked whether their teacher had said anything about the form of a doorway.
answer.outcome: They told him Rav Ashi said nothing at all.
answer.summary: Rav Aha, son of Rav Avya, came upon some of Rav Ashi's students and asked whether their master had said anything about the 'form of a doorway' used for an eruv. They replied that he had said nothing.
answer.missing: Any turn or consequence; it is a brief exchange reporting a teaching.

answer.actor: The son of Nehunya the well digger
answer.event: Despite his father's merit in digging wells, Nehunya's son died of thirst.
answer.turn: His father's merit did not protect him, which the rabbis explain by God being exacting with the righteous.
answer.outcome: He died.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abba reported that even though Nehunya dug wells for the public, his own son died of thirst. The rabbis take this as proof that God holds those closest to Him to a hair's-breadth standard.
answer.missing: Who Nehunya was and the preceding story about his daughter, which lies before segment [1]; the death is reported without circumstances.

answer.event: A heretic taunted Rabban Gamliel, citing Hosea, that God had performed halitza on Israel and abandoned them.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel pointed out the verse says 'from them', meaning Israel withdrew from God.
answer.outcome: He called the heretic a fool and showed such a halitza has no force.
answer.summary: A heretic told Rabban Gamliel that God had 'removed His shoe' from Israel, as a brother-in-law does to a widow, so the bond was over. Rabban Gamliel called him a fool: the verse says 'from them', so it is Israel who did the removing. A halitza performed by the widow's side on the brothers has no legal effect, so the bond stands.

answer.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna, who asked to meet him.
answer.turn: Rav Huna saw Rav Hamnuna's head was uncovered and learned it was because he was unmarried.
answer.outcome: Rav Huna turned away and told him not to see his face again until he married.
answer.summary: Rav Hisda kept telling Rav Huna what a great man Rav Hamnuna was, so Rav Huna asked to have him sent over. When he arrived, Rav Huna noticed he was not wearing the scholar's head-cloth and asked why; Rav Hamnuna said it was because he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to come before him again until he had a wife.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, Marei bar Mar, Rav Huna and his son Rabba
answer.event: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent Marei bar Mar to ask Rav Huna whether the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar on bills of divorce.
answer.turn: Before the question reached him, Rav Huna died.
answer.outcome: Rav Huna's son Rabba answered instead, reporting his father's tradition that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent a question through Marei bar Mar to Rav Huna: does the law follow Rabbi Elazar on divorce documents? Rav Huna died before the question arrived. His son Rabba answered in his place, saying his father had taught that the law does follow Rabbi Elazar, and that other scholars said the same in Rav's name.

answer.actor: a maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household
answer.event: The maidservant immersed herself in a ritual bath.
answer.turn: When she came up, a bone was found between her teeth.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi required her to immerse again.
answer.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household immersed in a ritual bath. After she came out, a bone was found stuck between her teeth. Rabbi ruled that the immersion did not count and she had to immerse again.

answer.event: Rav Yehuda, nearly blind, struggled hard to read documents himself before signing them.
answer.turn: Ulla told him it was unnecessary, since Rabbi Elazar and Rav Nahman had documents read to them by court scribes and then signed.
answer.summary: In his old age Rav Yehuda could barely see, yet he strained to read every document before signing it. Ulla told him he need not, because great authorities like Rabbi Elazar and Rav Nahman had scribes read documents aloud to them and then signed. The text does not say whether Rav Yehuda changed his practice; it moves on to a legal qualification.
answer.missing: Whether Rav Yehuda accepted Ulla's advice.

answer.actor: Bonyam ben Nunyam and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
answer.event: A wealthy man, Bonyam ben Nunyam, sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a gift of extremely fine linens.
answer.summary: A wealthy man named Bonyam ben Nunyam sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a gift of four kinds of fine linen. The fabrics were so thin they could be folded to the size of a nut or a pistachio, yet opened out large enough to clothe him. The passage then uses this to define a word.
answer.missing: Any turn or outcome; the gift is described but nothing follows from it.

answer.event: Colleagues challenged Ben Azzai for preaching the duty to have children while never marrying.
answer.outcome: Ben Azzai answered that his soul yearned for Torah and the world could be sustained by others.
answer.summary: Ben Azzai taught that failing to have children is like shedding blood. His colleagues pointed out that he preached this well but did not practice it, since he had never married. He replied that his soul longed only for Torah, and others could keep the world populated.

answer.actor: a man who came before Rabban Gamliel
answer.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel that on his wedding night he found no sign of virginity.
answer.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested the man had approached at an angle, explaining with a parable about a door that opens only if pushed aside.
answer.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel claiming that his new wife showed no sign of virginity. Rabban Gamliel suggested the man may have entered at an angle and so met no obstruction, comparing it to someone in the dark who finds a door open only because he pushed the bolt aside. The text does not say how the case was decided.
answer.missing: The outcome of the case.

answer.actor: Rava and Rav Mari bar Rahel
answer.event: Rava declared Rav Mari bar Rahel, son of a gentile father and Jewish mother, fit to marry into Israel and appointed him an official of Babylonia.
answer.summary: Rav Mari bar Rahel had a gentile father and a Jewish mother. Rava ruled that he was of acceptable lineage and even appointed him to an official post in Babylonia. The passage then justifies the appointment despite the rule that officials must come from among one's brethren.
answer.missing: Any turn or consequence; the passage is an event followed by legal justification.

answer.event: Rabbi Yohanan spent eighteen days with Rabbi Oshaya and his twelve students.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yohanan recalled spending eighteen days with Rabbi Oshaya, learning only one point about the Mishna's spelling from him. He also remembered that the study hall was so crowded that four students sat in each square cubit. The rest of the passage reconciles his conflicting statements.
answer.missing: A turn or ending; these are reminiscences rather than a story.

answer.event: While Ameimar sat in judgment a man removed a feather from his head; a man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva.
answer.turn: In each case the helper turned out to have a lawsuit to bring before the judge.
answer.outcome: Each judge declared himself disqualified from hearing that man's case.
answer.summary: A feather landed on Ameimar's head while he was judging, and a man came over and removed it. Ameimar asked what brought him, and the man said he had a case; Ameimar declared himself disqualified because of the favor. In a similar episode a man covered some spittle in front of Mar Ukva, turned out to have a case, and Mar Ukva likewise refused to judge it.

answer.event: Rabbi Zakkai recited a baraita before Rabbi Yohanan on the status of the area between side posts.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan rejected it.
answer.outcome: He told Rabbi Zakkai to go teach it outside, i.e., not in the study hall.
answer.summary: Rabbi Zakkai recited a teaching before Rabbi Yohanan that the area under a cross beam has a restricted legal status. Rabbi Yohanan dismissed it, telling him to go and teach it outside, meaning it did not belong in the study hall.

answer.event: While sitting before Rav Ashi, Ravina saw a man tying his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat and shouted at him.
answer.turn: The man ignored him, so Ravina pronounced him excommunicated in his teacher's presence, then worried this was disrespectful.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi reassured him that where God's name is desecrated, no deference is owed to a teacher.
answer.summary: Ravina was sitting with his teacher Rav Ashi when he saw a man tying his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat, which the Sages forbade. Ravina shouted at him, but the man paid no attention, so Ravina declared him excommunicated. Afterwards Ravina asked Rav Ashi whether acting like that in his presence was disrespectful. Rav Ashi told him that when God's name is being desecrated, honor for a teacher does not apply.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
answer.event: Rabbi Abbahu reported in Rabbi Yohanan's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka.
answer.turn: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi silently turned their faces away in disagreement.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abbahu sat and taught, in Rabbi Yohanan's name, that the law follows Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, sitting opposite him, turned their faces away to show they disagreed, without contradicting him aloud. The Gemara then debates who the speaker was and why they stayed silent.
answer.missing: Any resolution of the scene.

answer.event: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah the prophet and asked how a woman is a helper to a man.
answer.outcome: Elijah answered that she turns raw wheat and flax into bread and clothing, lighting up his eyes and standing him on his feet.
answer.summary: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah the prophet and asked him what the verse means by calling a wife a helper. Elijah answered that a man brings home wheat and flax, but he cannot chew raw wheat or wear raw flax; his wife turns them into bread and clothes. In that way she brightens his eyes and puts him on his feet.

answer.event: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi made prophetic pronouncements about places in Babylonia.
answer.turn: He revealed that the people of Bireta DeSatya had that day trapped fish on Shabbat, been excommunicated by Rabbi Ahai and become apostates, and that Adda bar Ahava was being circumcised.
answer.outcome: He announced that on that day Rav Yehuda was born in Babylonia.
answer.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi lay dying, he described places in Babylonia: one whose people were Ammonites, one full of mamzerim, one where two brothers swapped wives. He said that in Bireta DeSatya the people had that day caught fish on Shabbat from an overflowing ditch; Rabbi Ahai excommunicated them and they all abandoned Judaism. He said that in Akra DeAgma a boy, Adda bar Ahava, was that day sitting in Abraham's lap, newly circumcised, and that Rav Yehuda had just been born in Babylonia.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yohanan (told by Rabba bar bar Hana)
answer.event: Rabba bar bar Hana and others followed Rabbi Yohanan to eat the famous fruits of Genosar.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan ate a vast quantity, more than a three-se'a basket could hold.
answer.outcome: He then swore he had not yet tasted anything nourishing.
answer.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana recalled going with Rabbi Yohanan to eat the sweet fruits of Genosar. The group would take ten fruits each when they were a hundred people, or a hundred each when they were ten, and each hundred fruits overflowed a large basket. Rabbi Yohanan ate them all and then swore that he had not yet eaten anything that nourished him.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his sons
answer.event: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi called in his sons one at a time.
answer.turn: He gave his younger son Rabbi Shimon the orders of wisdom, and his older son Rabban Gamliel the procedures of the office of Nasi.
answer.outcome: He instructed Rabban Gamliel to lead with firmness and cast fear on his students.
answer.summary: As he was dying, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked for his younger son, Rabbi Shimon, and passed on to him the principles of wisdom. Then he asked for his older son, Rabban Gamliel, and handed him the procedures of the patriarchate, telling him to rule with authority and keep his students in awe. The deathbed scene began earlier and his death is not shown here.
answer.missing: The start of the deathbed narrative and its ending (Rabbi's death) lie outside the segments shown.

answer.actor: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov (and the students of Rav Huna)
answer.event: Rav Huna's long discourses left many of his students impotent; Rav Aha bar Ya'akov fell ill from holding back urine and was hung from the study hall's cedar column until a green substance came out of him.
answer.turn: The cure worked and spared him the fate of the others.
answer.outcome: He reported that of sixty elders, all became impotent except him, crediting the verse 'Wisdom preserves the life of him who has it.'
answer.summary: Several sages, Rav Giddel, Rav Helbo and Rav Sheshet, became impotent from sitting through Rav Huna's long discourses. Rav Aha bar Ya'akov caught the illness that comes from holding back urine, so they hung him from the cedar column of the study hall, and a green substance came out of him and he was healed. He later said that of the sixty elders present, all became impotent except him, because he had used wisdom to preserve himself.

answer.actor: a man testifying before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
answer.event: A man testified that someone had presumptive status as a Levite because he read second from the Torah.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi questioned whether the reading reflected Levite status or prominence, and the man answered that a priest had read before him.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated the person to Levite status on the man's word.
answer.summary: A man came to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and said that someone he knew had established himself as a Levite. Asked what he had seen, he said the person was called second to the Torah in the synagogue. When the rabbi asked whether that might only reflect the person's prominence, the man explained that a priest had read just before him, so he was called as a Levite. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi then granted him Levite status on that testimony.

answer.event: Absorbed in his learning, Nehemya walked beyond his Shabbat limit and could not return.
answer.turn: Rav Hisda brought his student's distress to Rav Nahman.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman instructed that a human partition be formed so Nehemya could walk back in.
answer.summary: Nehemya, son of Rav Hanilai, was so engrossed in study that he wandered outside his Shabbat boundary and was stuck. Rav Hisda told Rav Nahman that his student was in distress. Rav Nahman told him to have people line up as a human wall so Nehemya could walk back inside the boundary.
answer.missing: The text does not state explicitly that the partition was formed and that he reentered.

answer.event: Rabbi Zeira, who in Babylonia had believed the Rabbis disputed a ruling, went up to Eretz Yisrael and found Rabbi Asi teaching otherwise.
answer.turn: He discovered that, per Rabbi Yohanan, all agree on the point and the dispute concerns a different formula.
answer.summary: Rabbi Zeira recalled that in Babylonia they used to say the Rabbis disagreed with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about conditions phrased 'on the condition that.' When he went up to Eretz Yisrael, he found Rabbi Asi teaching in Rabbi Yohanan's name that everyone agrees on that point, and the dispute was only about 'from today and after death.'
answer.missing: It is a report of a correction of a tradition; there is no further event or ending beyond the discovery.

answer.event: Rava served drinks at his son's wedding; some sages stood for him and two, Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas, did not.
answer.turn: The two who stayed seated failed to honor him.
answer.outcome: Rava became angry and rebuked them, asking whether they alone were Sages and the others not.
answer.summary: At his son's wedding Rava personally poured drinks for the guests. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua stood up for him, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas son of Rav Hisda stayed seated. Rava grew angry and asked sarcastically whether those two were Sages and the ones who stood were not.

answer.actor: a man who came to Rabbi Yosei
answer.event: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether a widow could perform halitza within three months of her husband's death.
answer.turn: Told no, the man pushed back, asking what harm it would do.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yosei answered with a verse implying that only one eligible for levirate marriage may perform halitza.
answer.summary: A man came to Rabbi Yosei and asked whether halitza could be performed within three months of the husband's death. Rabbi Yosei said it could not. The man challenged him, asking what would be wrong with it, and Rabbi Yosei cited the verse 'if the man does not wish to take her,' teaching that halitza applies only where levirate marriage would be possible.

answer.event: Rabba issued a practical ruling about a bill of divorce found in a flax house in Pumbedita, following his own view.
answer.outcome: He ruled according to his halakha; the circumstances are disputed.
answer.summary: A bill of divorce was found in a flax house in Pumbedita, and Rabba ruled on it according to his own legal position. Traditions differ on the details: some say it was found where flax was soaked, a place caravans rarely pass, and others say where flax was sold, a busy place, but where no two men with the same name were known.
answer.missing: The actual ruling (return or not) and any consequence are not narrated; the passage is mostly about the disputed circumstances.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya
answer.event: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya visited and found him crying.
answer.turn: Rabbi Hiyya asked why he wept, since dying in tears is a bad omen.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi explained that he was crying over the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to fulfill.
answer.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi lay ill, Rabbi Hiyya came in and found him weeping. He asked his teacher why he was crying, reminding him of the teaching that dying while crying, or facing the wall, and the like, are bad signs. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi answered that he was weeping for the Torah and the commandments he would be unable to keep after death.

answer.actor: Pishon the camel driver and his wife
answer.event: Pishon's wife refused him (annulling the marriage) in his absence.
answer.turn: The refusal was allowed because Pishon had mismanaged her property.
answer.outcome: The Sages punished him measure for measure by validating the refusal.
answer.summary: In a debate between Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai, the case of Pishon the camel driver comes up: his wife refused him while he was not present. Beit Shammai explained that because Pishon had dealt dishonestly with her property, the Sages dealt with him in the same defective measure and let the refusal stand.
answer.missing: The incident is only cited as a precedent in an argument; how the refusal happened and its aftermath are not told.

answer.actor: a woman holding a bag of documents
answer.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents deposited with a woman, who claimed she had seized it from the deceased while he was alive for a debt.
answer.turn: Rav Nahman asked whether she had witnesses that the deceased demanded it in life and she refused, and she had none.
answer.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled her seizure counted as after death and was worthless.
answer.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and after the owner died his heirs came to claim it. She said she had taken it while he was still alive because he owed her money. Rav Nahman asked if she had witnesses that the man had asked for it back in his lifetime and she had refused; she did not. He therefore ruled that it was a seizure after death, which has no legal effect.

answer.actor: a widow at Rabbi Yehuda's court
answer.event: A woman came to testify before Rabbi Yehuda's court that her husband had died, and bystanders told her to lament, tear her clothes and loosen her hair.
answer.turn: The coaching was meant to satisfy Rabbi Yehuda's requirement that she appear grieving.
answer.summary: A woman came to Rabbi Yehuda's court to report her husband's death. People there told her to mourn openly, tear her clothes and unbind her hair so the court would believe her. They held she was permitted to remarry anyway, but wanted to make sure Rabbi Yehuda would also allow it.
answer.missing: The outcome of her case is not given.

answer.event: In a shepherds' village an inlet of the sea breached a courtyard wall, and the case came before Rav Yehuda.
answer.outcome: Rav Yehuda required only one standing board to permit carrying there.
answer.summary: Defending a ruling, Rav Yosef recalled a case in a shepherds' village where a narrow inlet of the sea broke through a courtyard wall. The question came to Rav Yehuda, who ruled that a single remaining board of wall was enough to permit carrying.
answer.missing: Only a precedent cited in argument; no developed narrative beyond the ruling.

answer.actor: the people of the Upper Galilee
answer.event: The people of the Upper Galilee bought a litra of meat every day for a poor man of noble birth from Tzippori.
answer.summary: The people of the Upper Galilee supported an impoverished man of noble background from Tzippori by buying him a litra of meat every day. The Gemara explains why this was remarkable: it was poultry, or it cost a fortune, or in such a small village an entire animal had to be slaughtered daily just for him.
answer.missing: It describes an ongoing practice; there is no turn or ending.

answer.event: Rav walked among the sheaves in a field and saw them waving in the wind.
answer.outcome: He told them that business was still better than farming.
answer.summary: Rav once went out among the standing grain and saw the stalks swaying. He addressed them, saying they could wave all they liked, but trade was more profitable than working the land.
answer.missing: A brief anecdote framing a saying; no real turn.

answer.actor: Levi, Ze'eiri and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
answer.event: On Shabbat, straw, fodder and water were brought to these sages through partitions formed by unwitting crowds.
answer.summary: Like Rava's attendants, who once brought flasks into his house behind the crowd returning from his lecture, others used crowds as partitions: straw was brought in for Levi, fodder for Ze'eiri, and water for Rav Shimi bar Hiyya.
answer.missing: Bare list of incidents with no turn or ending; the explanation of the method comes from the preceding context.

answer.event: A student of Rabbi Eliezer was liable to death by burning for his sins.
answer.turn: The Rabbis decided to spare him.
answer.outcome: They let him alone because he had served a great man.
answer.summary: Rabbi Eliezer had a student who had sinned so gravely that he deserved death by burning. The Rabbis said to leave him alone, because he had served a great person.
answer.missing: What he did and what happened to him afterward are not told.

answer.event: A man who had set his Shabbat-boundary eiruv with onions to reach Tiv'in came before Rabbi Meir in Ardiska.
answer.turn: Rabbi Meir held that an onion eiruv is invalid, so the man was outside his limit.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Meir confined him to his four cubits.
answer.summary: Rabbi Meir was spending Shabbat in Ardiska when a man came to him and said he had made his boundary eiruv with onions so he could walk to Tiv'in. Rabbi Meir considered such an eiruv invalid, meaning the man had already passed his Shabbat limit. He ordered him to stay within his four cubits.

answer.event: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question about who reads from the Torah after the priest and Levite.
answer.turn: He did not know the answer and went to ask Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha gave him the order of precedence for Torah readers.
answer.summary: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question: after the priest and the Levite, who is called to read the Torah? He did not know, so he went and asked Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, who told him the order: scholars appointed as community leaders, then scholars fit to be appointed, then sons of such leaders, then synagogue heads and everyone else.
answer.missing: The passage segment alone breaks off mid-question; the rest of the episode is in the following context segment, and it is mainly a legal answer.

answer.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down to let his mother step on him getting into and out of bed, and boasted of it in the study hall.
answer.turn: The sages told him he had not reached even half the honor due her.
answer.outcome: He was humbled with the example of a mother who throws a purse into the sea without being shamed by her son.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tarfon honored his mother by bending down so she could climb onto him to get into and out of bed. He came and praised himself for this in the study hall. The sages answered that he had not reached even half of the honor due to her: had she ever thrown his purse into the sea before his eyes without his embarrassing her?

answer.actor: a man's daughter and the orphan heirs
answer.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter, but the heirs divided the estate without giving her one.
answer.turn: Rav Yosef thought the case matched the mishna where each heir can deflect the claim, but Abaye showed the tree is a shared obligation.
answer.outcome: Abaye ruled they must give her a palm tree and redivide the estate from the start.
answer.summary: A man said in his will that his daughter should get a palm tree. His sons divided the estate and gave her nothing. Rav Yosef thought each brother could claim the tree was in someone else's share, as in the mishna, but Abaye disagreed: here the obligation rests on all of them. His remedy: give her a palm tree and divide the inheritance again from the beginning.

answer.event: The two schools disputed for two and a half years whether it would have been better for man not to have been created.
answer.turn: They took a vote.
answer.outcome: They concluded it would have been better not to be created, but now that man exists he should examine his deeds.
answer.summary: For two and a half years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argued over whether humanity would have been better off never created. In the end they counted votes and decided it would have been better not to be created; but since we are here, a person should examine his deeds.
answer.missing: The dispute itself is only a stated opinion; there is little narrative beyond the duration and the vote.

answer.event: A ritual bath in Yavne presumed full was measured and found deficient, and Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva disputed whether purifications done in it were valid.
answer.turn: Rabbi Akiva produced an analysis showing the bath resembles a blemished priest, not one of flawed lineage.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Tarfon conceded, saying anyone who separates from Akiva separates from life.
answer.summary: A reservoir in Yavne thought to hold enough water for a ritual bath was measured and found short. Rabbi Tarfon ruled that the purifications done in it stood, while Rabbi Akiva ruled them void, and they traded arguments and parables about priests discovered to be disqualified. Rabbi Akiva then showed why the bath is like a blemished priest, whose service is invalid. Rabbi Tarfon accepted it and told him that whoever parts from him parts from life.

answer.event: Ravin went as agent to betroth a woman for his son but betrothed her to himself.
answer.turn: Her family refused to give her to the son, and Ravin feared someone else would betroth her while he went to report back.
answer.outcome: He married her himself.
answer.summary: Ravin the Pious went to betroth a woman on his son's behalf but ended up betrothing her to himself. Her family would not give her to his son, only to him. Rather than first telling his son, he acted at once, fearing that in the meantime another man would come and betroth her.

answer.event: Ravina examined a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia during the lifetime of his teacher Rav Ashi.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi challenged him, and Ravina cited Rav Hamnuna's precedent; when Rav Ashi disputed the tradition, Ravina reconciled both versions.
answer.outcome: Ravina defended himself as Rav Ashi's disciple-colleague, permitted to rule in another town.
answer.summary: Ravina checked a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia while his teacher Rav Ashi was alive, and Rav Ashi asked why he had done it. Ravina pointed to Rav Hamnuna, who ruled in another town during his teacher Rav Hisda's life. Rav Ashi replied that the tradition was that Hamnuna did not rule; Ravina answered that both traditions were true, since Hamnuna was Rav Hisda's disciple-colleague, and so was Ravina to Rav Ashi.

answer.actor: Rabbi Banai and the orphan daughters
answer.event: Rabbi Banai held movable property belonging to orphans, and the daughters came before Shmuel.
answer.outcome: Shmuel told Rabbi Banai to go and support the daughters from it.
answer.summary: Rabbi Banai, brother of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, was holding movable property that belonged to some orphans. The orphan daughters brought the matter to Shmuel, who told Rabbi Banai to go and provide for them from it.
answer.missing: It is cited as a precedent; there is no real turn, and the purpose of the payment is left for the legal discussion.

answer.event: A case about establishing priestly status came before Rabbi Yohanan, and Reish Lakish again demanded proof from the threshing floor.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yohanan gave the same retort Rabbi Elazar had given earlier, revealing that Elazar had been quoting him.
answer.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yohanan by name.
answer.summary: Earlier, when Reish Lakish insisted a man's priesthood be proven by receiving teruma at the threshing floor, Rabbi Elazar objected: if there is no threshing floor, does priesthood cease? Later, sitting before Rabbi Yohanan, the same kind of case arose, Reish Lakish asked the same question, and Rabbi Yohanan answered with the very same words. Reish Lakish looked harshly at Rabbi Elazar and said: you heard this from the blacksmith's son and did not tell us in his name?

answer.event: Bar Shatya, who was intermittently insane, sold property, and two pairs of witnesses contradicted each other about his state at the sale.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi held that the two testimonies cancel out.
answer.outcome: The land stayed in Bar Shatya's possession.
answer.summary: A man called Bar Shatya, who sometimes went insane, sold some property. Two witnesses said he sold it while sane; two others said he was insane at the time. Rav Ashi ruled that the testimonies cancel each other, so the land remained in Bar Shatya's hands.

answer.event: A man grabbed coins from someone else and threw them to a woman washing her feet, declaring her betrothed to him.
answer.turn: The case came before Rava.
answer.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal void, since the coins were stolen and the owner had not given up on them.
answer.summary: A woman was washing her feet in a basin of water when a man snatched some coins from another person, tossed them to her, and said, 'You are betrothed to me.' The case came to Rava, who ruled that no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view that a robbery victim gives up hope, so the coins were not the man's and the betrothal had no effect.

answer.actor: Rabbi Abbahu and his attendant Rabbi Nahum
answer.event: While walking leaning on Rabbi Nahum's shoulder, Rabbi Abbahu answered his attendant's questions about when the halakha follows an unattributed mishna.
answer.turn: Rabbi Nahum challenged him with a mishna on combs whose unattributed ruling is not followed.
answer.outcome: He was told that mishna is an exception, since Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish said it is not an authoritative mishna.
answer.summary: Rabbi Abbahu used to walk leaning on the shoulder of his attendant Rabbi Nahum, who would gather rulings from him on the way. Nahum asked a series of questions on how to rule when a mishna or baraita gives an unattributed opinion alongside a dispute, and Abbahu answered each. When Nahum challenged him with a mishna about flax and wool combs that is not followed, he was told that mishna is an exception, declared non-authoritative by Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish.
answer.missing: Beyond the walking frame, this is a legal question-and-answer with no event; the translation also names Rabbi Hiyya as respondent in the later part, which is unclear.

answer.event: A woman gave birth twelve months after her husband went overseas.
answer.outcome: Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child legitimate, presuming a delayed pregnancy.
answer.summary: A woman's husband went overseas, and she gave birth twelve months after he left. Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child legitimate, treating the husband as the father on the view that a pregnancy can be delayed.
answer.missing: The case is only cited as a precedent; there is no development beyond the ruling.

answer.event: Ameimar permitted Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi challenged him, noting that three schools did not teach the ruling he relied on.
answer.outcome: Ameimar did not accept the objection, because he had heard the ruling directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.
answer.summary: Ameimar allowed Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza, a place of doubtful lineage. Rav Ashi questioned him: the schools of Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid did not teach the ruling that all lands are presumed of good lineage. Ameimar stood by his decision, since he had heard it directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.

answer.event: Rabbi Tavla visited Mehoza and saw a bolt hanging from the side of a door.
answer.outcome: He said nothing to the people there.
answer.summary: Rabbi Tavla came to Mehoza and saw a door bolt hanging from the side of a doorway, not tied to the door. He said nothing against it; the Gemara explains it was the kind of bolt lifted by its rope.
answer.missing: It is a brief observation cited as evidence; there is no turn or development.

answer.event: Yehuda bar Mareimar escorted Rav Pappa to the house of Abba of Sura for his son's marriage contract but did not want to enter.
answer.turn: Pressed to enter, he sat silent; Abba of Sura took the silence for anger and wrote all his property into the dowry.
answer.outcome: Yehuda said he did not want this, but told Abba not to retract and make himself a man who goes back on his word.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa went to have the marriage contract written for his son, who was marrying into the family of Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to accompany him but would not go inside. Yehuda explained that his mere presence would pressure the father into a larger dowry; Rav Pappa made him enter anyway. Yehuda sat in silence, and Abba of Sura, thinking he was angry, signed over everything he owned as a dowry. When Yehuda said he had not wanted that, Abba offered to retract, but Yehuda told him not to become a man who goes back on his word.

answer.event: An incident arose involving loss caused by voiding a sold promissory note.
answer.turn: Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to issue an unequivocal ruling.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi had the full value of the note collected, as for damaging a beam meant for a sculpture.
answer.summary: A case came up in which a creditor forgave a loan after selling the note, causing loss to the buyer. Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to rule decisively, and Rav Ashi made the creditor pay the full value of the note.
answer.missing: The facts of the incident are given only by reference to the preceding legal discussion; no parties or details are named.

answer.event: In a case before him, Rabbi ruled (or meant to rule) according to the Rabbis of the mishna, and Perata objected that this would leave the court no more power than an ordinary person.
answer.turn: Perata's objection persuaded Rabbi.
answer.outcome: Rabbi reversed his ruling (in Rav Safra's version, he never carried it out).
answer.summary: Rav Dimi reported a case in which Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled according to the Rabbis of the mishna. Perata, grandson of Rabbi Perata the Great, objected that if so, the court would have no more power than an ordinary person. Rabbi then reversed his ruling. Rav Safra told it slightly differently: Rabbi only wanted to rule that way, and after the objection he did not do it.

answer.event: A yavam and yevama who both said they had not consummated the levirate marriage came before Rava, and he ordered halitza for her.
answer.turn: Rav Sherevya cited a baraita requiring both a bill of divorce and halitza.
answer.outcome: Rava accepted it and retracted his ruling.
answer.summary: A yavam and his yevama came before Rava, both saying they had never consummated the levirate marriage. Rava told the scholars to arrange halitza for her and settle her case. Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires both a bill of divorce and halitza. Rava answered that if the baraita teaches it, so be it, and withdrew his ruling.

answer.event: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba, who died childless, and Rabban Gamliel then took her rival wife in levirate marriage.
answer.summary: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba. Abba died without children, and Rabban Gamliel took his daughter's rival wife in levirate marriage. The Gemara cites this as an incident, but only as evidence in a legal argument; no turn or ending follows.
answer.missing: Any turn or consequence of the incident; the text only reports the act.

answer.event: Doubting a ruling Rav Beruna attributed to Shmuel, Rabbi Elazar had Rav Beruna show him Shmuel's lodging and asked Shmuel directly, who confirmed it.
answer.turn: Rabbi Elazar challenged Shmuel with Shmuel's own earlier statement that contradicted the ruling.
answer.outcome: Shmuel was silent and did not answer.
answer.summary: Rav Beruna was reciting a ruling of Shmuel. Rabbi Elazar doubted Shmuel had said it, so he asked to be shown Shmuel's lodging and went to ask him himself. Shmuel confirmed it. Rabbi Elazar then pointed to another statement of Shmuel's that seemed to contradict it, and Shmuel fell silent.

answer.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (and the people of Bireta DeSatya)
answer.event: On his deathbed Rabbi made prophetic statements about places in Babylonia, including that the people of Bireta DeSatya had that day turned away from God.
answer.turn: They had trapped fish on Shabbat when a ditch overflowed, and Rabbi Ahai excommunicated them.
answer.outcome: They all became apostates; Rabbi also announced that Adda bar Ahava was circumcised that day and Rav Yehuda was born.
answer.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi lay dying, he made prophetic pronouncements about Babylonian places, such as towns whose people were Ammonites or mamzerim. He said that on that day the people of Bireta DeSatya had turned from God: a fish ditch overflowed and they caught the fish on Shabbat, Rabbi Ahai excommunicated them, and they all abandoned Judaism. He added that Adda bar Ahava of Akra DeAgma was being circumcised that day and that Rav Yehuda had just been born.

answer.event: On three questions of double liability, Rabbi Hiyya and Bar Kappara each jumped up and swore by the Temple service that he had heard his opposite ruling from Rabbi, then each argued his case.
answer.summary: Rabbi Hiyya and Bar Kappara disagreed over whether someone who breaks two prohibitions in one act is liable twice or once. Three times, each jumped up and swore by the Temple service that he had heard his own ruling from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and each then argued his reasoning. The scene of the competing oaths is vivid, but it never resolves. What follows is the Gemara's legal analysis.
answer.missing: A resolution of the confrontation; the text moves into legal analysis.

answer.event: Ten men carried a woman out on a bier, as if she were dead, and had intercourse with her.
answer.summary: Rav ruled that a woman may not be secluded even with ten immoral men, and an incident is cited as proof. Ten men carried a woman out on a bier as if she were dead and had intercourse with her. The report is a single bare line given as evidence for the ruling.
answer.missing: Who was involved and any aftermath; the incident is told in one line.

answer.event: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain ruling, and his student Abaye reminded him that he had taught it to them himself.
answer.turn: It is revealed that Rav Yosef had forgotten his own teaching.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a certain ruling. His student Abaye told him that he himself had taught it to them, and said where he had taught it. The passage does not say how Rav Yosef responded.
answer.missing: Rav Yosef's reaction; the explanation that his illness made him forget comes only from the translator's gloss.

answer.event: Rav Safra raised objections to a ruling Abaye was reciting in Rav Yosef's name, and Abaye could not answer.
answer.turn: Abaye reported the objections to Rav Yosef.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef told him the answer he should have given: members of a Paschal group are vigilant.
answer.summary: Abaye was teaching a ruling of Rav Yosef when Rav Safra challenged it with mishnayot. Abaye deflected the first challenge but could not answer the second and fell silent. He went to Rav Yosef and told him what Rav Safra had said. Rav Yosef asked why he had not answered that members of a Paschal lamb group are vigilant.

answer.actor: A man and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya
answer.event: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags, and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examined it before Rav to see whether it was worth a peruta.
answer.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags. Sitting before Rav, Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examined the bundle to see whether it was worth a peruta, which would decide whether the betrothal was valid. The text does not say what he found, and the Gemara moves on to a legal question.
answer.missing: The result of the examination.

answer.event: Rabbi Eliezer missed the study hall, met Rabbi Asi, and asked him what had been said there.
answer.turn: Rabbi Asi told him Rabbi Yohanan ruled like Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Eliezer asked whether that meant only one authority disagreed.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Asi said yes and cited a baraita.
answer.summary: One day Rabbi Eliezer did not go to the study hall. He met Rabbi Asi and asked what had been said there. Rabbi Asi said Rabbi Yohanan had ruled according to Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Eliezer asked whether only a single authority disagreed, and Rabbi Asi confirmed it with a baraita. It is a frame for a legal exchange rather than a full story.

answer.actor: Rava and Rav Natan bar Ami
answer.event: Rava compelled the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity and collected four hundred dinars from him.
answer.outcome: Four hundred dinars were collected for charity.
answer.summary: To show that a court may compel a wealthy man, the Gemara cites a case: Rava forced the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity and took four hundred dinars from him. The case is told in a single line as a precedent.
answer.missing: Any background or reaction; the case is a bare precedent.

answer.actor: Rav Avya and his wife, the sister of Rami bar Hama
answer.event: When the couple's marriage contract was lost, they came before Rav Yosef, who first said they could continue without one for a while.
answer.turn: Abaye objected that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's decrees.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef told Rav Avya to go and write her a new marriage contract.
answer.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya, and her marriage contract was lost. They asked Rav Yosef, who said the strict view was Rabbi Meir's, while the Rabbis allow a man to stay with his wife for two or three years without one. Abaye objected that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir in his decrees. Rav Yosef then told Rav Avya to go and write her a new contract.

answer.event: At his son Abba Mar's wedding, Rav Pappa poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda.
answer.turn: Rav Yitzhak did not stand up for him.
answer.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa was serving drinks to the guests at his son Abba Mar's wedding. When he poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, Rav Yitzhak did not stand for him, and Rav Pappa was offended. The Gemara concludes that even when a rabbi forgoes his honor, some gesture of respect is still required.

answer.event: When Rabbi Elazar moved to Eretz Yisrael, was ordained, and joined the council for intercalating the calendar, he each time declared that he had escaped another curse.
answer.turn: Each step freed him from one of the three curses in Ezekiel on false prophets.
answer.outcome: He had escaped all three curses.
answer.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael, he said he had been spared one curse. When he was ordained, he said he had been spared two, and when he was seated on the council that intercalated the calendar, he said three. The three were Ezekiel's curses on false prophets: shut out of the council, the register of Israel, and the land of Israel.

answer.event: Rav Yosef taught a ruling in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and Rav Beivai told the Sages not to listen to him.
answer.turn: Rav Beivai said he had given Rav Yosef the teaching himself, in Rav Adda bar Ahava's name, and that it was about 'many', not 'Rabbi'.
answer.outcome: Rav Yosef exclaimed 'Master of Abraham!' and admitted he had confused 'rabbim' with 'Rabbi'.
answer.summary: Rav Yosef taught a ruling about courtyards in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. Rav Beivai told the Sages not to listen: he had taught it to Rav Yosef himself, in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava, and it concerned the word 'many' (rabbim). Rav Yosef exclaimed 'Master of Abraham!' and admitted he had confused 'rabbim' with 'Rabbi'.

answer.event: When the sons of Yudan the maidservant were freed, Rav Aha bar Ya'akov allowed them to marry each other's wives.
answer.turn: Rava challenged him that Rav Sheshet had prohibited exactly this.
answer.outcome: Rav Aha stood by his ruling: Rav Sheshet prohibits and I permit.
answer.summary: The sons of a freed maidservant named Yudan wanted to marry each other's former wives, and Rav Aha bar Ya'akov permitted it. Rava confronted him, pointing out that Rav Sheshet had forbidden such marriages. Rav Aha replied bluntly that Rav Sheshet forbids it and he permits it.

answer.event: A marriage contract whose scribe's handwriting and one witness's signature were recognized was brought before Rabbi Abbahu, who intended to validate it.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yirmeya objected that the mishna requires the scribe to have signed, not merely written it.
answer.summary: A marriage contract came before Rabbi Abbahu; people recognized the scribe's handwriting and the signature of one witness, so he was inclined to declare it valid. Rabbi Yirmeya objected that the rule speaks of a scribe who signed, so handwriting alone is not enough. The text does not say what Rabbi Abbahu finally decided.
answer.missing: Rabbi Abbahu's final decision on the document.

answer.event: Rabbi Yehoshua was asked how the law rules on the rival wife of a daughter and whether to follow Beit Shammai or Beit Hillel.
answer.turn: He refused to decide, saying he feared the two great 'mountains' would crush his skull.
answer.outcome: Instead he testified that two great Jerusalem families descended from rival wives and produced High Priests.
answer.summary: Sages asked Rabbi Yehoshua which school's ruling to follow on the rival wife of a daughter. He declined, asking why they were putting his head between two great mountains, and said he feared for his skull. He offered instead his testimony that two prominent Jerusalem families were descendants of such rival wives and had produced High Priests.

answer.event: Visiting his son-in-law Rav Hisda, Rav Aha bar Abba took his granddaughter onto his lap.
answer.turn: Rav Hisda objected that she might be betrothed; Rav Aha countered that betrothing a minor violates Rav's ruling, and Rav Hisda retorted that holding a woman violates Shmuel's ruling.
answer.outcome: Rav Aha answered that he follows Shmuel's other teaching: everything is permitted for the sake of Heaven.
answer.summary: Rav Aha bar Abba came to the house of his son-in-law Rav Hisda and put his little granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether he wasn't worried she might already be betrothed; Rav Aha shot back that then Rav Hisda would have broken Rav's rule against betrothing a minor daughter. Rav Hisda countered that Rav Aha was breaking Shmuel's rule against making use of a woman, and Rav Aha closed the exchange by citing another teaching of Shmuel: all is permitted when done for the sake of Heaven.

answer.actor: Rav Yehuda, son of Rav Yehezkel
answer.event: While Rav Yehezkel taught a mishna to his son Rami, his other son Rav Yehuda told him he was teaching it wrongly.
answer.turn: Father and son argued over the version, and Rav Yehuda answered his father's objection.
answer.outcome: Shmuel rebuked Rav Yehuda for speaking to his father that way, citing the proper respectful way to correct a parent.
answer.summary: Rav Yehezkel was teaching his son Rami a ruling about mixed groups of condemned criminals. His other son, Rav Yehuda, interrupted: 'Father, don't teach it that way,' and proposed a different version; the father raised an objection and the son answered it. Later Shmuel scolded Rav Yehuda, calling him 'big-toothed one,' and told him not to speak to his father like that, since a son should correct a parent only indirectly by quoting the verse.

answer.event: A heretic mocked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya as a 'man of thorns', citing a verse that Israel's best are like briers.
answer.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and pointed to the end of the verse.
answer.outcome: He reinterpreted the verse as praise: the best of Israel protect it like a thorn hedge, and will crush the nations.
answer.summary: A heretic taunted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya, calling him a man of thorns because a verse says the best of Israel are like a brier. Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and told him to read the rest of the verse. He then turned the insult around: just as thorns seal a breach in a fence, the best of Israel protect their people, and they will one day grind the nations underfoot.

answer.event: Rabbi Ami publicly declared a man in his neighborhood to be a mamzer.
answer.turn: The man went about weeping.
answer.outcome: Rabbi Ami consoled him: by making it known, he had given him life.
answer.summary: A man living near Rabbi Ami was publicly declared by him to be a mamzer. The man walked around weeping. Rabbi Ami told him he had actually given him life, since a known mamzer and his line survive.

answer.event: The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi sent two Sages to examine them.
answer.turn: When women told them 'your husbands are coming', they replied 'let them be your husbands'.
answer.outcome: Rabbi declared there is no greater refusal than this.
answer.summary: The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent a pair of Sages to look into the matter. When some women pointed and said, 'Look, your husbands are coming,' the young wives answered, 'Let them be your husbands.' Rabbi ruled that there is no stronger act of refusal than that.

answer.event: In Mar Shmuel's days there was a lentil bread which he threw to his dog.
answer.turn: Even the dog would not eat it.
answer.summary: In the days of Mar Shmuel there was a loaf of lentil bread. Shmuel threw it to his dog, and the dog refused to eat it. It is cited only as evidence about whether such bread is edible.
answer.missing: Any further development; the incident is only a brief cited anecdote.

answer.event: A mourning woman removed her husband's body from his grave.
answer.summary: The text alludes to a well-known incident in which a woman, while mourning, took her husband out of his grave. It is mentioned only as proof that temptation strikes even in mourning; the Hebrew does not tell the story itself.
answer.missing: The actual story (her liaison with the guard and why she disinterred her husband) is only supplied by the translator's gloss, not by the text.

answer.event: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi to testify about a matter, and Rav Ashi at first said he did not remember even after Rav Kahana prompted him.
answer.turn: Rav Ashi later remembered and testified, but saw Rav Kahana hesitate, fearing he had influenced the testimony.
answer.outcome: Rav Ashi assured him he had not relied on his prompting but had worked to remember it himself.
answer.summary: Rav Ashi knew some testimony relevant to Rav Kahana. Asked if he remembered it, he said no, and even when Rav Kahana described what happened, Rav Ashi said he did not know. Eventually Rav Ashi remembered and testified, and when he saw Rav Kahana hesitating, he told him: 'Do you think I am relying on you? I made the effort and remembered it myself.'

answer.event: A woman from Mehoza married to a man from Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract, and hearing her accent he ruled by Mehoza's custom.
answer.turn: They told him she was marrying into Neharde'a.
answer.outcome: He reversed himself and ruled by Neharde'a's custom, following Shmuel.
answer.summary: A woman from Mehoza, married to a man from Neharde'a, came with her family before Rav Nahman. Hearing her Mehoza accent, he said that Babylonia follows Rav's ruling. They pointed out that she was marrying into Neharde'a, and he answered that in that case Neharde'a follows Shmuel.

answer.event: Rav Pappa went to write the marriage contract for his son's match with the family of Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to greet him.
answer.turn: At the door, Yehuda bar Mareimar took his leave and seemed reluctant to enter, so Rav Pappa asked what was on his mind, suggesting a teaching of Shmuel about not taking part in transferring inheritance.
answer.summary: Rav Pappa arranged a marriage for his son into the family of Abba of Sura and went to supervise the writing of the bride's marriage contract. Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to honor him but turned to leave at the doorway; Rav Pappa invited him in, saw he was unwilling, and asked whether it was because of Shmuel's warning against helping divert an inheritance. The resolution is not in the text shown.
answer.missing: How the exchange ended (Yehuda bar Mareimar's answer and whether he entered).

answer.actor: a certain man and his heirs
answer.event: A man instructed in his will that a dowry be given to his daughter.
answer.turn: The cost of a dowry dropped, leaving a difference.
answer.outcome: Rav Idi bar Avin ruled the savings go to the sons.
answer.summary: A man left instructions that his daughter be given a dowry. By the time it was provided, dowry goods had become cheaper. Rav Idi bar Avin ruled that the leftover money belongs to the sons, not the daughter. It is a legal case reported mainly for its ruling.

answer.event: In a shepherds' village an alleyway ending in a backyard came before Rav Yehuda.
answer.outcome: He required nothing to permit carrying there.
